100.Title: Principles of Financial Accounting
100.Description: The course is designed to provide an understanding of financial accounting fundamentals for prospective users of corporate financial information, such as investors, creditors, employees, and other stakeholders (e.g., suppliers, customers). The course focuses on understanding how economic events such as operating activities, corporate investments, and financing transactions are recorded in the three main financial statements (i.e., the income statement, balance sheet, and statement of cash flows). The main emphasis of this course is placed on the basic framework of accounting so as to provide the student with an understanding of the fundamental accounting principles and concepts. A heavy reliance will be placed on problem solving and practical analyses to achieve the aforementioned level of understanding. Students will develop the technical skills needed to analyze financial statements and disclosures for use in financial analysis. Students will also learn how accounting standards and managerial incentives affect the financial reporting process. The tools and skills you learn in this course will help you throughout your professional career and your life.

2101.Title: Introduction to Finance and Accounting
2101.Description: The course is designed to provide a basic understanding of financial accounting as a foundation for Accounting and Finance course in the masters program. The course focuses on understanding how frequently occurring economic events are recorded in the three main financial statements (i.e., the income statement, balance sheet, and statement of changes in equity). The main emphasis of this course is placed on the basic framework of accounting so as to provide the student with an understanding of the fundamental accounting principles and concepts. Assignments and quizzes would be used to assess successful completion of this course.

5101.Title: Financial Management and Accounting
5101.Description: This course is divided into three modules covering financial accounting, managerial accounting and foundations of finance. Module 1Accounting is the universal language of business. Sound accounting knowledge is important for understanding and shaping capital markets. Users of financial reports include investors, creditors, managers, unions, and government agencies. This course introduces the concepts of financial accounting with emphasis on the interpretation of financial statements and how financial statement data can be used to assess and manage value creation activities. This module will help students understand what accounting can do for managers—the decision-makers. The objective of this module is to give students an understanding of current financial accounting and reporting environment, taking into account the diverse interests of both external users and management. Module 2The second part of this course will cover analysis of financial statements using some basic techniques including horizontal and vertical analysis, ratio analysis and industry averages. Module 3This module will lay the foundations of finance with an emphasis on applications vital for corporate managers. Major financial decisions made by corporate managers both within the firm and in their interactions with investors will be covered in this module. Essential in most of these decisions is the process of valuation, which will be emphasized throughout this module. Topics include criteria for making investment decisions, valuation of financial assets and liabilities, relationships between risk and return, capital structure choice, payout policy, and risk management.

100.Title: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
100.Description: This course is designed to introduce students to the methods, theories, and concepts of cultural anthropology. Drawing on ethnographic accounts from all parts of the world we will investigate how people in other cultures define themselves and others, make sense of their world, and organize their lives. We will look at past and contemporary ways that anthropologists have thought about culture. You will be confronted by a great diversity of human lifestyles, beliefs and behaviors, and faced with the problem of teasing out general statements about humanity from these different ethnographic accounts. Through this comparative and broad- based approach, we will also learn something about ourselves and our own culture. As the semester progresses, you will reflect not only on the topics of the day, but also what the culture and society of peoples in places as distant as Africa, Melanesia and Asia tell us about our own lives. The course will also consider how anthropological perspectives promote a more nuanced insight to issues of colonialism, culture change, race, immigration, new media, and globalization.

253.Title: Women's Lives Across Cultures
253.Description: This course focuses on contemporary women’s lives in different economic and cultural settings. It examines their common experiences and some of the global processes which link them. The assigned readings and films this term deal with women living in the Sudan, Mali, Nicaragua, the U.S., China, India, France, Thailand, Pakistan, Papa New Guinea, Afghanistan, Korea, Lebanon, and Japan, as well as women who are displaced around the world.During the term we will examine some of the typical roles women play in society; the cultural rationales and structural conditions behind practices like female circumcision and women’s acceptance of and resistance to such practices; the globalization of work, sex, and ideas of female beauty; the influence different forms of social organization have on women’s lives; media images of women; and women’s social activism and development work on behalf of women. We will also spend a significant portion of the course critically deconstructing powder dynamics within the feminist movement, examining the impacts of colonization, neoimperialism, and neoliberal on contemporary feminisms, as well as the significant contributions of black, postcolonial, and indigenous feminists towards gender, sexuality, and race-based rights.As anthropologists we will be striving to acquire an insider’s perspective, but we will also examine the opinions of outsiders who typically view other women’s lives through the filter of their own culture. We will be reading about and watching films which show both women’s victimization as well as their agency and collective efforts to create better lives for themselves and for their societies and future generations.

268.Title: Introduction to Anthropology of Religion
268.Description: The study of religion has been central to anthropology since its inception, and the source of many of its most important comparative concepts and debates. In this course we begin with the long-running discussion around the definition of religion as a category before exploring other key themes in the anthropology of religion, such as how religions are practiced, embodied, experienced and understood. Examples are drawn from a variety of different religions as well as from studies of the secular, and assessments include an ethnographic research project.

320.Title: Qualitative Research Methods
320.Description: Even in the age of big data and AI, qualitative methods remain critical to understanding the world. QRM captures how we experience the world, imbues relationships with significance, and gives meaning to objects. Instead of what they should look like in text and theory, qualitative methods allow us to see how institutions, religions, and markets operate in practice. Moving beyond the normative cases presented by aggregate numbers, qualitative science uncovers the contingent and anomalous, offering a nuanced understanding of lived lives. It gives us access to the affects, beliefs, and emotional investments that make social existence possible.However, some of the greatest strengths of qualitative research methods - using experience as data and privileging the contingent - also present the biggest pedagogical challenges. How do we prepare for a field that is always in motion? In the field, are we to act as flies on the wall, recording everything that happens before us, or should we look for specific, ethnographically rich conversations, expressions, emotions, and actions? How do we layer the various, contingent conversations and practices we record to recognize patterns? When do these patterns become strong enough to speak back to larger structures, such as the nation-state, capitalism, imperialism, and liberalismThe course offers practical experience as the best approach to learning qualitative research methods. It helps students build their methodological toolkit through immersion in the field. The semester will be divided into different parts. We start by examining recent scholarship on Pakistan to outline the kinds of questions qualitative researchers are asking and the approaches they take. By the end of this phase, students should form their research groups. In the next phase, workshops, training sessions, and writing assignments provide a foundation for the field research by outlining a clear research question and field plan for each group. In the subsequent phase, we focus on training and practicing one specific methodological approach each week. The data collected through these different practices should enable each group to develop an ethnographically rich and conceptually meaningful final project. In the last phase, we come back to the classroom to workshop our research findings and think more deeply about presentation and writing.

333.Title: Ethics of Romantic Love
333.Description: This course takes an interdisciplinary approach towards exploring ethical problems in the context of romantic relationships as well as the feelings, thoughts, and actions that precede and succeed them. It is broadly divided in four modules that explore the lifecycle of romantic love through concepts such as morality, patriarchy, modernity, coloniality, capitalism, difference, violation, rationality, and temporality. The course shifts between primarily philosophical and anthropological texts each week with the goal of introducing you to historical and contemporary theories and practices of romantic ethics. The ethnographic studies assigned are mostly drawn from Muslim-majority contexts in order to limit the scope of the course and for juxtaposing and contextualizing Islamic ethics of romance in broader discourses on the same. Assigned readings – primarily peer reviewed journal articles and book chapters – will be supplemented during class with media examples such as clips from TV shows and feature films, documentaries, songs, poems, op-eds, podcasts, educational videos, magazine articles, and interviews. Course assignments will hone your critical thinking, reading, writing, speaking, and listening skills separately and together with opportunities for you to explore, develop, and share your interests and experiences with your peers. Readings and lectures are designed to accommodate students from diverse disciplines and with no prior academic training on the course topics.

453.Title: Sex and the State
453.Description: Just how political is the personal? Is the government really in your bedroom, how did they getthere, and should they stay? How come all conversations about gender feel like conversations aboutthe nation’s honor? Join us this semester to examine the critical role that sex and sexuality have playedin the development of the modern nation-state, as well as how the emergence of political modernityhas transformed our understanding of sex and sexuality in fundamental ways.This reading and writing intensive course will be rooted in anthropological concepts andmethods, while traversing widely across ethnography, critical theory, and history. Thinking through anon-exhaustive cross-section of global debates, including hijab laws, abortion politics, and imperialhomonationalism, we will interrogate the entanglements of gender, religion, nation, and colonialpower. In tandem with ethnographic deep-dives, we will read Lauren Berlant, Judith Butler, VeenaDas, Michel Foucault, Saba Mahmood, Jasbir Puar, Joan W. Scott, and other scholars.

101.Title: Introductory Biology
101.Description: Introductory biology aims to provide a broad overview of biology as it stands today, exposing students to a variety of topics in modern molecular and cellular biology. The course is divided into four modules:1. Macromolecules and Cell Biology:We start with an introduction to the molecules of life and how they are organised into a cell, the basic unit of life in all living organisms. Students learn how cells communicate with each other, how they divide, and how they produce and consume energy. 2. Genes and DevelopmentThe course then focuses on the organisation of genetic material and how various molecular, genetic and biochemical processes underlie the functioning of cells from replicating their genetic material for cell division to accurately producing essential proteins during development. 3. Omics and Systems Biology:This module provides an overview of how modern biology is reliant on generation and analysis of big data and how this data can be utilised for a better understanding of biological systems.4. Human Diseases and Drug Discovery:In the end, we discuss how communicable and non-communicable human diseases are caused and how understanding the molecular mechanisms of these diseases allows us to develop more effective drugs. Manipulating genetic materials is at the heart of advances in life sciences that we see today from biomedical to agricultural sciences. This module also provides an overview of how the genetic makeup of organisms can be manipulated in the laboratory.

216.Title: Molecular Biology
216.Description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to molecular biology and is designed for students interested in learning molecularmechanisms which control cellular processes in eukaryotes and prokaryotes. Topics include structure of nucleic acids and proteins, organizationof genes, genomes, chromatin and chromosomes, DNA replication, repair, recombination, transcription, mRNA processing, protein synthesis andturnover, control of gene expression, signal transduction pathways, non-coding RNAs, evolution of biopolymers and origin of life.

221.Title: Genetics
221.Description: The intellectual framework of this course will introduce students to basic concepts in genetics and epigenetics. Both genetic and epigenetic inheritance patterns will be introduced with an emphasis how they influence our development. Different modules will cover classical genetics based on Mendelian laws and gene interactions which explain deviations from Mendel’s laws. In addition, microbial genetics will be explained to help understand how fundamentals of gene regulation were discovered. During this course, students will learn in great detail how forward and reverse genetics approaches in different model systems are employed to understand cellular function. Moreover, human genetics module will explain how genetics plays a major role by using alleles in humans to understand disease and development. Last but not the least, understanding quantitative genetics and population genetics will explain how mutagenic traits are investigated and how genes may evolve at a population level. How genetics has helped us understanding molecular and biochemical pathways of development is an important subject of this course.

300.Title: Methods in Cell and Molecular Biology
300.Description: This lab course is designed to introduce fundamentals of molecular and biochemical tools using in a molecular biology lab to understand function of a cell. It kicks off with a brief introduction to bioinformatics comprising of exercises and hands on experiments involving homology searches (both DNA and protein searches) and primer design for various applications. Major part of lab comprises of independent modules in molecular biology, biochemistry and genetics which introduce students to molecular cloning, agrobacterium mediated transformations, protein expression and purification through chromatography and enzymatic assays. In addition, classical and molecular genetics module involves experiments using Drosophila to understand various concepts of development, chromatin and gene regulation. A thirty minutes pre-lab lecture is followed by hands on lab experiments which will expose students to cutting edge ideas and questions of molecular and cell biology.

313.Title: Cell Biology
313.Description: Cells are the most complicated entities known to humans and constitute every living organism in this world from bacteria to humans. Understanding the complex workings of different cells is at the heart of understanding how our bodies work. Cell biology, therefore, is one of the most fundamental subjects of biology. This course is organized into 4 modules that will help students understand how eukaryotic cells are organized and how they function. The first module will provide students with in depth understanding of the dynamic functions of cell membrane and various components of the cytoplast like endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and chloroplasts. The second module will cover intercellular interactions, cell signaling, and extra cellular environment. The third module will introduce students to cell division and differentiation. In this module students will learn about cytoskeleton, cell cycle regulation, cell death, cancer and stem cells. The course will conclude after discussing application of above mentioned principles in specialized immune cells that defend their host against invasion of pathogens

331.Title: Computational Biology II
331.Description: The primary focus of the course is to understand theoretical foundation of some of the most widely used computational biology techniques. The principles and methods for pair-wise and multiple sequence analysis using hidden Markov models, phylogenetic analysis, protein sequence analysis and structure prediction are extensively covered. In addition systems biology is introduced at a glance with a significant amount of time spent on microarray analysis. The tutorials will provide hands-on training of programming in R and MATLAB with the aim of developing problem solving skills in computational biology research using scripting languages

524.Title: Evolution
524.Description: Evolutionary ideas link different fields of biology. This course provides an evolutionary context to understand biology. We will review the history of evolutionary thoughts, the forces of evolution, and the need for an extended evolutionary synthesis theory. We will also study the application of evolutionary studies to medicine and agriculture.

541.Title: Epidemiology and Methods in Clinical Research
541.Description: The course is an elective course and will provide fundamental understanding of epidemiology, the basic science of Public Health. An important objective would be to familiarize students of the distribution of health outcomes across population, where ethnicity, cultural norms and values play a critical role in adaptation of a specific health behavior. At population level, focus will be on the use of appropriate epidemiological methods for investigating disease outbreaks in case of infectious diseases, disease prevalence, incidence and risk factors associated with the acquisition and progression of diseases, both infectious and chronic and finally evaluation of interventions for lowering disease burden. Topics included will be measurement of disease frequency and association, study design, bias, confounding and causality. To make this more multi-disciplinary, the topic will be further expanded on use of molecular and cell biology tools for diagnosis, screening, and risk assessment of diseases in the community. Students will apply theoretical knowledge on real-world public health problems through case studies and project presentations. Towards the end of the course, students will be able to critically assess epidemiologic research and apply evidence-based approaches to disease prevention and control.

314.Title: Quantum Chemistry

This course also discusses the significance of wavefunctions, operators and eigenvalues, and how the position, momentum and energy of a particle are related with them in quantum mechanics. It also covers the examples of harmonic oscillator and the rigid rotator for explaining the vibrational and rotational spectra of molecules respectively. Exact solution of Schrodinger equation for the hydrogen-like atoms and approximation methods used for the multi-electron atoms are also discussed. Periodic properties of elements are discussed in light of the electron-electron repulsion terms, radial distribution functions, the most probable radii shielding and penetration, , and the energies of orbitals. This course also discusses the formation of molecular orbitals in molecules from the linear combination of atomic orbitals, hybridization of atomic orbitals, ¿-electron approximation for conjugated hydrocarbons and the Huckel molecular orbital theory for aromatic compounds.

324.Title: Inorganic Chemistry I

The topics covered will include bonding, trends in periodic properties, molecular symmetry and its relationship to spectra, acid-base & donor-acceptor chemistry, Solid state chemistry, chemistry of the main group elements, and coordination chemistry. 532.Title: Chemistry of Biomolecules

Although these biomolecules are major part of a typical biochemistry course; however, the Chemistry of Biomolecules deals mostly with the structural and mechanistic details of biomolecules and their reactions at the level of atoms and bonds. The study of biomolecules in this context have become crucial to tackle the modern challenges of biological sciences such as medicine, pharmacology and even biochemistry itself. Additionally, since majority of biomolecules are organic molecules, the Chemistry of Biomolecules can also motivate an organic chemist to mimic the chemistry of nature to design bioinspired-materials, -catalysts and -reactions. Chemistry of Biomolecules is thus a course for future leaders in the area of biological sciences as well as organic chemistry. In this course, fundamental concepts of organic chemistry will be utilized to explain how enzymes catalyze reactions of metabolic pathways and why metabolites react the way they do. Thus, Chemistry of Biomolecules aims not only to expand the chemical research on structures, synthesis and kinetics in a biological direction, but also prepare senior undergraduates and graduate students of chemistry and biology for the challenging area of drug-design, -discovery, and -delivery.

1000.Title: Adab and Literature
1000.Description: This course introduces students to the many ways in which stories can be told and meaning can and has historically been made with a particular focus on narratives of displacement and homelessness. The course asks students to think about the interlinked questions of home, migration, and displacement from the perspective of their relevance to contemporary questions using frameworks of comparative literary and cultural studies. Over the semester, we will work with a range of narratives—poems, stories, essays, films, and images—to think not just about how we can grapple with questions of home and displacement, but in fact, how essential these questions have been for humanistic thinking in our part of the world. We begin each module with an examination of the classical Western literary formation and then trace how this formation changes during the colonial encounter, and finally what spaces and voices it inhabits in the postcolonial moment. Our method is always informed by the question of contexts: where does a text come from? How does it offer meaning to those who read or view it? What kinds of pasts and presents inform a story? What are the various ways of interpreting a text?

Through close engagement with screenplays, film scenes, and selected readings, students will examine how narrative ideas translate into visual form, and how those translations carry meaning, ideology, and feeling. The course covers structure, conflict, character, dialogue, subtext, sound, composition, tone, and duration, with particular attention to how these elements work differently across genres, platforms, and cultural contexts. 2119.Title: Mechanics of Fiction
2119.Description: In this course we will read at a variety of short stories (and a movie) with one aim: to understand the strategies and techniques that writers have used to make their fictional worlds “real”. We will be discussing in detail things that obsess writers: voice, character, words, sentences, use of detail and dialogue, narrative, atmosphere, setting, imagery, metaphor, and the like. We will also look at stories (and some critical essays) from Urdu, which will help us grapple with questions of translatability and bilinguality that are central to writers from our part of the world. The reading list is drawn from a wide variety of literary texts so as to enable us to sympathize with a broad range of sensibilities, regardless of our own natural inclinations. from conventional realism and its variants (see Chekhov, Paley, Grover) to the more contemporary ‘postmodern’ fiction which upends conventional expectations from literary fiction (see Calvino, Le Guin, David Foster Wallace, Masud, etc). Please note that this is a writing course through reading. It is built on the premise that writers – or those who want to write – are, first and foremost, tireless and passionate readers of literary texts. In this course, there will be repeated and relentless emphasis on close reading, fussing over little details and looking at them in terms of the role they play in the fictional world they exist. The last couple of weeks will be dedicated to workshopping student writings and reflecting on the writing process. Our guides through this course will be mainly writers who are also critics. Aside from this, we will read essays by other writers on the craft of writing.

2133.Title: Fountain of the Sun: Rumi’s Masnavi and Divan
2133.Description: Jalal al-Din Muhammad Balkhi Rumi, a Persian poet and Sufi master born in 1207, has been the best-selling poet in the United States for more than two decades now. Rumi is revered as one of the world’s greatest poets & spiritual leaders by devotees of Sufism, adepts of new-age spirituality and those with a mystical orientation towards religion. This course, through a selection of Rumi’s Masnavi & Divan, is aimed at providing a comprehensive understanding of Rumi’s literary and spiritual legacy in our times. The course shall explore the text of Masnavi and Divan from multiple angles, especially but not limited to existentialist, phenomenological, psychological and spiritual ones. Extractions from the texts would be used to hone the skills of the learners to analyze the merits of figurative speech and how Rumi transformed the power of metaphor to incorporate the repressed realities of the world around him. While Masnavi & Divan remain at the core of this course, using the primary sources of Rumi’s biography, it will also attempt to highlight the early years of Rumi’s life and discuss the training he received by his mentors in order to explain what made him the most influential figure in the realm of poetry and Sufism. The course will also pay a close attention to Rumi’s global impact on mysticism and world literature

2143.Title: Modern Urdu Novel
2143.Description: This course aims to navigate the modern phase of the Urdu novel. Although the Urdu novel emerged in the nineteenth century through the Indian imagination’s engagement with colonial modernity, it assumed a distinctly new direction in the postcolonial period. It moved beyond functioning merely as a literary instrument of nation-building and began to question the very notion of nation shaped under the restrictive imaginative regimes of colonial modernity, a shift powerfully represented in Qurratulain Hyder’s Aag Ka Darya.Since the 1960s, the Urdu novel has increasingly explored the historical construction of personal and collective identities through narratives set across both ancient and modern periods of India, the Middle East, and Central Asia. This mode of exploration differs significantly from conventional historical fiction. Rather than simply recreating the past, these novels interrogate history itself—its structures, silences, and ideological uses. In this way, the modern Urdu novel developed a distinctive form and aesthetic of its own.Abdullah Hussain’s Qaid (Imprisonment) explores the historical transformations of post-Partition Punjabi society in Pakistan. In Jamila Hashmi’s Chehra ba Chehra, Ru ba Ru (Face to Face), resistance at the threshold of history is examined through a narrative set in nineteenth-century Iran, based on the life of Qurratulain Tahira. Similarly, Fahmida Riaz’s Qila-e-Faramoshi (Fortress of Forgetfulness) engages with the theme of resistance through the life of Mazdak in fifth-century Iran.These novels do not reflect a nostalgic fascination with the past; rather, they seek to recover and expand the concepts of time and history that were narrowed under colonial rule. Colonial discourse often represented India as a land without history, or at best acknowledged its ancient past only as something dead and disconnected from the present. The modern Urdu novel challenges these colonial constructions of history and reclaims historical consciousness in a critical and imaginative way. In this sense, these novels are fundamentally decolonial.At the same time, they never sacrifice the artistic integrity of fiction. Even a novella like Nambardar ka Neela (The Lumberdar’s Neela), though not directly based on historical events, carries deep political significance. Its central figure, Neela—the ox—functions symbolically, and its true importance emerges through the underlying structures of power and authority within the narrative.

2214.Title: Mechanics of Film
2214.Description: “Cinema is a matter of what's in the frame and what's out.” – Martin ScorseseThis course examines the art of filmmaking and visual storytelling through the close reading of films and the stories they tell. Beginning with the origins of the moving image, it traces the development of cinematic language from early cinema and Soviet montage through Classical Hollywood and Italian Neorealism to the cinemas of the Global South, before turning to digital filmmaking.With a focus on the core techniques of narrative film, such as mise-en-scène, cinematography, editing, sound, and narrative form, the course pairs the study of craft with historical and cultural context, anchored by key filmmakers and films. Alongside foundational figures such as Sergei Eisenstein, Orson Welles, Vittorio De Sica, and Satyajit Ray, it engages with female authorship and filmmakers from Asia, Africa, and Latin America, whose work has both shaped and challenged the medium. At the same time, students will produce work in the medium they are studying, immersing themselves in the moving image and its visual language. By the end of the course, students will emerge as active viewers, trained in the language of film, with an understanding of how cinematic technique and narrative structure work together to construct meaning on screen, and equipped to apply that understanding to their own work.

The course contains three ‘sprints’ to accommodate students at any level of drawing abilities. It begins with developing an explorative sketchbook practice that focuses on drawing by hand and creating a unique visual voice – sensibilities vital for artists to develop with the advent of AI-generated art. During the weekly assignments segment of the course, students will learn to create in a collaborative environment while learning skills that allow them to transfer sketches from traditional surfaces to digital devices for completion. The course will culminate in a final, guided project where students translate a short story of their choice from words to pictures. The selected short story will function as the springboard through which students explore, learn, and share visual concepts and create a series of visuals for a specific illustration market. 3414.Title: The Past is a Foreign Country: Memory, Myth and Historical Storytelling
3414.Description: Modern historical consciousness begins with a strange and unsettling realization: the past is not simply earlier—it is fundamentally different. To think historically is to recognize that people once lived inside worlds of meaning that no longer fully translate into our own. Their assumptions, emotions, moral orders, and political imaginations do not sit quietly behind us as ‘background’; they resist us, flicker at the edges of understanding, and occasionally refuse to make sense at all. The past, in this sense, is not a record—it is an encounter with alterity.And yet, we never meet the past directly. We inherit it through stories.This course takes these conditions seriously and turns them into questions. How is the past made to feel foreign in the first place—and through what narrative strategies is that distance sustained or softened? When does storytelling bring us closer to the past, and when does it sharpen its strangeness? What happens when fiction, myth, and archive begin to speak in the same voice? Can the past ever be fully translated, or does something always remain resistant? And finally, what does it mean not to overcome the past’s foreignness, but to learn how to think with it?Bridging history and literary studies, in this course we shall examine these questions through a small selection of works—a combination of chronicle, myth, colonial text, fiction, and film—where storytelling becomes a mode of historical thinking. With a South Asian emphasis the course will explore how myth, memory, and storytelling have long coexisted and competed in our part of the world. Works like Rajatarangini and Padmavat reveal earlier narrative traditions in which history, legend and literary imagination are inseparable. In the modern period, this entanglement intensifies; Anandamath by Bankim Chandra demonstrates how the historical novel can turn the past into a charged instrument of nationalist imagination, collective identity and political aspiration.Similarly, around sites such as the Somnath temple, competing narratives of origin, conquest, and loss circulate across historiography, politics, and fiction. Here, the past fractures into irreconcilable stories: the same figure appears, by turns, as founder, invader, liberator, or symbol. In Sita Betrayed, Qurratulain Hyder reworks epic memory through fiction, unsettling inherited mythologies and revealing how gender and historical consciousness are continually rewritten through narrative form.In its final movement, the course turns to visual culture through artwork and a museum visit, where paintings—silent in themselves—acquire meaning only within narrative frames. Across these various encounters, students learn not to resolve the past’s foreignness, but to inhabit it—long enough to see that the past does not wait to be found. It takes shape only in the telling, and in every telling, it is made again—and made otherwise.

202.Description: Data structures are abstractions for storing data in a computer system and form an essential building block in the design of efficient algorithms. 501.Title: Applied Probability
501.Description: This is an intermediate level course focusing on the application of probability theory to science and engineering disciplines.The first portion of the course reviews the basic probability theory with some examples chosen from science and engineering. Laterportion of the course deals with moderately advanced topics that signify the use of probability theory in these disciplines.The topics covered in the course should help the students building a background for understanding and conducting research incomputer and data sciences, estimation and learning, and other more general engineering problems. In particular, we will discussrandom variables and expectations, joint and conditional distributions, random processes, queueing systems and Markov chains,confidence intervals, and prediction/learning/estimation theory.One important application area we will cover in the course is queueing theory.Why queuing theory? Any system (e.g., a web server, a customer service center) that has finite capacity and provides a servicecan potentially be modeled using queuing theory, which provides us with tools to predict system performance as well as designsystems that achieve high performance. For example, using queuing theory we can answer questions such as “What is the averagedelay experienced by requests arriving at a web server?” and “Given demand and a size of a given hospital, how many doctorsshould be hired to ensure that the no patient waits for longer than 10mins with high, say 98 percent, probability?”).We will also provide a brief introduction to machine learning, another important application area that has gained recent popularity.Why machine learning? Computers are increasingly being used as data analysis tools to obtain insights from the enormous amountsof data that is being collected in a variety of fields (now referred to as “big data”). Probability theory is now used as one of thekey methods for designing new algorithms to model such data, allowing, for example, a computer to make predictions aboutuncertain or new events. A use case would be to predict the weather tomorrow given weather data for past 10 years.A key goal of this course is to act as a bridge between the theoretical foundations of probability and its applications.

5603.Title: Cloud Development
5603.Description: Cloud Computing adaptation has been on the rise for over a decade now with enterprises and the industry. It offers great savings with infrastructure as service and continues to grow its software service offerings as well ranging from something as simple as static website hosting to the bleeding edge technology like Gen AI as a service. While old enterprises continue to migrate to the cloud, new companies are starting on cloud. Knowing this and that the future will only see growth in this area, its imperative that students understand what the cloud means, what it offers, different tradeoffs when opting between their offerings and making well informed design decisions.In this course students will learn about cloud using the AWS cloud platform, build detailed knowledge of some of the most commonly used and important services that complete design and implementation of a software solution. They will be guided how to accelerate their knowledge of these services in a professional environment and what to consider while working on commercial software solutions with clients and companies.The course lectures start off with the basic components of a software system and the hardware/network it lives on. Then after a short refresher, it would draw parallels between that and an equivalent cloud setup. Once the larger picture is clear, we would go deeper into each of the area, talk about alternates, considerations, costing, high availability, monitoring, auditing, and other standard industry practices. The course will, with its limited credit hours, also touch on aspects like infra as code, disaster recovery, automation, and DevOps.
5603.Specific Scheduling Information: Open for CS-MS and AI-MS in Phase II & Add/Drop Period.

5604.Title: AI-Driven Software Engineering
5604.Description: This research-oriented course focuses on the emerging fields of AI for Software Engineering (AI4SE) and Software Engineering for AI (SE4AI). It examines how artificial intelligence techniques—such as large language models and search-based optimization—are being applied to improve software development, analysis, and maintenance, as well as how sound software engineering practices are enhancing the development of AI systems at organizations such as Microsoft, Google, GitHub, Meta, and Huawei. The course emphasizes research skill development in the field of empirical software engineering, with the primary goal of producing a short, publication-ready research paper by the end of the term. As part of the curriculum, students will explore the research contributions, including Christian Bird and Nachiappan Nagappan at Microsoft, Caitlin Sadowski at Google, Eddie Aftandilian at GitHub, Mark Harman at Meta, Ahmed Hassan at Huawei, Prem Devanbu at UC Davis, Christian Kästner at CMU, Federica Sarro at UCL, Danny Dig at Colorado, Safwat Hassan at UFToronto, and Gail Murphy at UBC.

5803.Title: Applied Cryptography
5803.Description: This course explores the theory, design, and implementation of modern cryptographic systems used to secure information in real-world applications. Beginning with foundational concepts such as modular arithmetic, historical ciphers, and number theory, the course advances through the design and analysis of stream ciphers, block ciphers (including AES), and public-key cryptographic algorithms like RSA and Diffie-Hellman. Students will explore cryptographic primitives and protocols—such as digital signatures, hash functions, and message authentication codes—while also analyzing system-level threats, including implementation attacks and man-in-the-middle vulnerabilities. Real-world use cases are explored in depth, including Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) security and the protection of implantable medical devices against battery depletion and other attacks. The course concludes with student-led presentations on advanced topics such as elliptic curve and post-quantum cryptography, providing a comprehensive understanding of cryptography in both theory and practice.

5812.Title: Introduction to Blockchain: Technology and Applications
5812.Description: This course focuses on the foundational technologies behind blockchain. We will cover the concepts of distributed ledger, consensus mechanisms, authentication techniques, and relevant protocols. The course will provide case studies of blockchain applications such as cryptocurrencies, supply chain management, and B2B/B2C/C2C scenarios. The course will also provide hands-on experience with building and deploying smart contracts.

582.Title: Distributed Systems
582.Description: "The goal of this course is to study the fundamentals of distributed systems, and synthesize the design principles for building large-scale distributed systems. In this course students will first gain an understanding of the principles and techniques behind the design of distributed systems, such as locking, concurrency, consistency, scheduling, fault tolerance and communication across the network. Second, through real world case studies students will learn how these concepts are applied in various large-scale distributed systems (e.g., Internet, Cloud datacenters, Big data processing systems like Spark, Distributed machine learning systems like Parameter Server and Caching systems like Memcached). Third, students will gain practical experience designing, implementing, and debugging distributed systems through a set of programming assignments"

The course provides the students with current trends and future insight to modern computer architecture design.

6315.Title: Multi-agent Systems
6315.Description: "The course is about algorithmic game theory and its applications in engineering, economics, and social domains. Game theory is the study of interacting decision makers where each decision maker is acting in a selfish manner. In engineering applications, the decision makers can be robots or other computing machines that are required to achieve some desired global objective. In economics applications, the decision makers can be firms that are competing in a market for their own profit maximization. In social domain, the players can be humans interacting in societal situations like traffic or social good applications.The course will cover the basic framework for strategic games and its various manifestations. Topics include matrix games, extensive form games, mixed strategies, repeated games, Bayesian games, and cooperative games. The course will continue with an application of game theory as a design tool for multiagent systems, i.e., systems that consist of a collection of programmable decision-making components. Game theory as a design tool has applications in diverse domains like online advertisements and auctions, modeling of social phenomena, distributed optimization, resource allocation, throughput maximization in computer networks, and demand management in smart grids."

112.Description: Problem solving is an essential skill that managers use in their decision-making processes. In view of the pervasive use of computers, the contemporary manager must be aware of the tools and techniques that support problem-solving and decision-making in the modern business environment. 203.Title: Probability and Statistics
203.Description: This course is designed to provide students majoring in management and finance with an elementary introduction to probability and statistics with applications. Both descriptive and inferential statistics are covered. We first review techniques for organizing and presenting the raw data and elementary probability theory. Next, we discuss various techniques to make inferences. Along with probability theory, sampling distribution and central limit theorem shall be discussed. The idea of central limit theorem will naturally lead towards the confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for mean and proportion. We follow this discussion with single and multiple regression analysis, model building, design of experiments and categorical data analysis. The course also aims to give a hands-on experience with using a statistical package R for carrying out data analysis. The main objective of the course is to provide students with the foundations of statistical inference mostly used in business and economics.

231.Title: Operations Management
231.Description: Operations transform resource or data inputs into desired goods, services, or results to create value for customers and the manufacturer/service provider. An operation in automotive industry may involve an automotive assembly. In banking, an operation may involve providing teller services to the customers. Similarly, at McDonalds an operation may involve producing Big Mac or french fries. A primary objective of any manager (regardless of the industry type) is to design, plan, execute, and continuously improve the operation— for which he/she is responsible for, in a cost-effective manner. A thorough understanding of the intricacies involved is a requisite for cost effective and efficient management of manufacturing and service operations.This is core business course that aims to provide an overview of fundamental operations management concepts as well as an in-depth understanding of proven techniques and best practices. During the course, the similarities and differences in operations management for various types of commercial sectors (such as manufacturing, services, etc.) shall be specifically highlighted.After completing this course student will potentially be able to understand key concepts in operations management and would be able to choose and apply operations management tools and techniques.

325.Title: Business Data Management
325.Description: In Business Data Management, students will learn the steps involved in developing a database system for analyses. They will develop an understanding of data preparation operations such as extraction, cleaning, transforming, loading and updating. They will learn business data modeling, allowing them to develop conceptual data models based on business problem statements along with creating a database schema using graphical tools and data definition language. Students will also manage database and perform data analyses by extracting information from the database using Structured Query Language (SQL). Finally, students will be exposed to the concepts of data warehousing and Online Analytical Processing (OLAP), along with an introduction to data privacy and security. One important component of the course will be the group project in which students will apply the knowledge acquired during the course by building a database system for analytics from scratch. Here they will extract online data, clean and transform it and load it in a relational database to perform data mining.

327.Title: Risk Management Process
327.Description: Risk management helps identify and analyze potential issues that could arise during a project or process. Risk analysis is used to reduce the impact of a negative event, compare benefits to risks, plan responses to address emergencies or other adverse events and mitigate or eliminate risks during a process. This course constitutes a study of risk assessment and management techniques, methods, and models used in the industry to minimize, control, and communicate risks, including conducting various risk management protocols. The students will learn practical applications of risk-based planning and risk management tools essential to the success of any program. They will also grasp the principles to communicate the process and its value in avoiding catastrophic outcomes. We’ll rely on simulations and case studies to deliver key concepts. “The recommended textbook takes a close look at misused and misapplied basic analysis methods and shows how some of the most popular risk management methods are no better than astrology! Using examples from the 2008 credit crisis, natural disasters, outsourcing to China, engineering disasters, and more, Hubbard reveals critical flaws in risk management methods; and shows how all these problems can be fixed. The solutions involve combinations of scientifically proven and frequently used methods from nuclear power, exploratory oil, and other areas of business and government. Finally, Hubbard explains how new forms of collaboration across all industries and government can improve risk management in every field.”

333.Title: Supply Chain and Logistics Management
333.Description: In today’s world of competitiveness supply-chains compete with supply-chains rather than individual organizations. Individual organizations cannot survive by maximizing their local benefits rather they have to develop linkages and collaborate with others in order to survive and get a bigger pie of the market share. Moreover, globalization brings its own challenges and opportunities that impact the performance of each partner within a supply chain. In the wake of these challenges, many local and multinational organizations in Pakistan and abroad have established their own supply chain planning and execution functions. Whether that be manufacturing sector (FMCGs, Textiles, Engineering goods, Defense etc.), services sector (Financial Services, Retailing, Food Industry etc.) or social development sector (natural disaster management, social mobilization etc.), the need of supply chain management has become imperative.

335.Title: Transportation and Logistics Management
335.Description: In today’s world of competitiveness individual organizations cannot survive by maximizing their local benefits; rather they have to develop linkages and collaborate with others in order to survive and get a bigger pie of the market share. Moreover, globalization brings its own challenges and opportunities that impact the performance of each partner within a supply chain.Considering the fact that logistics and supply chain management are now firmly established as critical business concerns. Many companies have appointed Directors and Vice-Presidents who are responsible for ensuring the cost-effective operation of the ‘end-to-end pipeline’ that links the supply side of the business with the end market. Supply chains today operate in a world where the rate of change continues to increase. As we enter an era that some have termed ‘The New Industrial Revolution’ much of the conventional wisdom that has been the basis for supply chain design and thinking will have to be questioned. Hence, the emphasis of this course will be on the need to develop logistics and supply chain solutions that are flexible and capable of adapting quickly to changes in the business environment. By the end of this course, the students should be able to understand, arrange, and coordinate the movement of goods and material in a supply chain.

420.Title: Business Analytics
420.Description: Throughout the Management Science degree, students have already been exposed to a number of statistical and analytical techniques such as decision analysis, regression, optimization, etc. However, before these can be practically deployed as “business analytics” or “business intelligence” (i.e. analytical tools and techniques that rely on a business‘ data to solve business problems) three things remain. These three things, described as follows, are the focus of this course: 1. Understanding the systems and their organization to support business analytics: Why use a data warehouse on top of a regular database? What components and processes have todays organizations developed to practically deal with capture and dissemination of business intelligence? (The top left circle in the diagram above) 2. Data mining techniques: Certain analytical techniques rely on computerized “machine learning”. There are supervised versus unsupervised learning and classification versus association. This course will approach the subject from a business perspective: what is the objective of the technique? What business problems can it resolve? And mostly hands-on application of the tools. (the overlap between information systems circle and statistics circle) 3. Integration of business analytics topics: No real-world problem comes with a label such as “Use regression or the a priori algorithm.” After studying data-mining techniques, the student should now have a full menu of approaches at their disposal. It is the intelligence of the business professional that guides them in choosing which technique to employ. Hence, this course aims to help students practice this judgment call at a basic level in various situations essentially using a case-based approach.

6501.Title: Applied Data Analysis
6501.Description: This course is designed to develop data analytic skills of students to become sophisticated producers and consumers of empirically grounded practices in businesses and public policy. The course will help students to interpret evidence clearly and concisely to improve the speed, reliability, and quality of decisions. The concept learned in this class should help students identify opportunities in which data analytics can be used to improve performance and support important decisions. To gain a greater understanding and familiarity with the growing use of “Big Data” in decision making, students will work intensively with real world data, drawing from examples in business and public policy, to develop the skills to use data in making informed decisions.The students are expected to work on STATA to explore real world problems/questions, develop hypothesis and perform basic statistical analysis on the questions of interest they chose for empirical projects using real world data sets, such as Pakistan Demographic and Health Surveys (PDHS), Health Insurance Subsidy Program (HISP), Pakistan Labor Force Surveys (PLFS), and Pakistan Enterprise Surveys (PES). 8301.Title: Seminar in Operations and Supply Chain Strategy
8301.Description: The course will examine various thematic areas within the discipline of operations and supply chain strategy (OSCS) both in terms of basic concepts and current theoretical debates. The first four weeks of the course comprise of the research in operations management in general, editorial policies of top tiered journals that publish empirical research in operations management, evolution of OSCS as a discipline and the use of theories within OSCS. The remaining course is designed around three paradigms that firms utilize in operations for gaining competitive edge namely: operating capabilities, best practices, and strategic choices. Each paradigm covers a set of thematic areas within operations and supply chain strategy. At the same time, a few topics that have emerged in the recent years are also discussed.

111.Title: Principles of Microeconomics
111.Description: This course teaches basic microeconomic concepts and their implications for individuals and firms. Attention will be paid to understanding the decision-making process of households, business firms and government, and consequent allocation of resource and price determination under different market structures. Market equilibrium conditions will be discussed in the short run and the long run under various market models. This course is meant to foster critical evaluation of standard economic concepts such as scarcity and choice, demand and supply, cost and productions, government intervention & market failure, price mechanism, the efficient allocation of scarce resources and concludes with game theory

121.Title: Principles of Macroeconomics
121.Description: "Overall Theme To provide the students with an introduction to the basic macroeconomic principles; to enable students to appreciate the workings of real (labour and goods) and asset/money markets and the nature of equilibrium in each market; to emphasize the role of macroeconomic policies that affect internal and external deficits, inflation and growth of per capita income. Throughout the course a focus will be on ‘critical thinking’ to analyze macroeconomic problems.  Focus areas The major areas of focus will be the inputs market, goods market, money/asset market, and economic growth. Business cycles will also be discussed and linked to macroeconomic policy debate issues of ‘active’ versus ‘passive’ and ‘rules’ versus discretion. The equilibrium IS-LM, ADAS model will be covered with some basic applications, providing a smooth transition to Intermediate Macroeconomics.  The course is pitched at the core principles level so is based on the understanding that students have at least attained the some basic macroeconomics knowledge equivalent to that covered in any primary Economics course.  Upon completion of the course it is expected that students should be able to: (a) understand the structure of the economy and theories of macroeconomics at a level appropriate for a first year economics graduate; (b) understand the key links between the goods market, input markets and money markets.  (c) understand the macroeconomic models underlying the goods, input and money market, as well as the IS-LM, AD-AS framework"

203.Title: Reading Marx with Dickens
203.Description: This course will focus on the historical epoch - the industrial revolution - that shaped the writings of Karl Marx and Charles Dickens. Where Marx uses the ideas of class consciousness, exploitation, and social injustice to rally the working class,. Dickens' novels quite movingly depict the subjective experiences of working individuals - particularly children and young adults. Students will read a selection of Marx's writings together with a suitable text from Dickens, exploring how social theory and literature can reinforce each other in illuminating processes of historical change.

240.Title: Development Economics
240.Description: This course examines the process of economic development, including the determinants of underdevelopment and poverty. We will focus on describing and understanding the many problems faced by developing countries and their citizens. Throughout the course, we will discuss policy implications of the topics we explore. We begin with an overview of economic development and models economists use to understand the process of economic development. Next, we consider the impediments to development and how they can potentially be addressed. The emphasis throughout the course will be largely on microeconomic (health, education) issues and how to address these. At the same time, we will also look at some other problems such as migration and urbanization

244.Title: Introduction to Environmental Economics
244.Description: This course introduces students to the economic principles, concepts, and methodologies required to understand the relationship between human decisions and the environment. Our planet is a closed environmental system with a limited capacity to assimilate the harmful byproducts of economic activity. Interventions to improve the environment entail a tradeoff between economic activity and environmental quality. In this course we will learn how economic agents allocate scarce resources among competing uses, what impact such allocations have on the environment, and how social planners and private agents can reallocate resources to achieve socially desirable outcomes. We will explore the measurement of environmental costs and benefits, the application of cost-benefit analysis to environmental problems, alternative policy instruments for pollution control, and the implications of economic growth and climate change for a sustainable environment in developing countries.TEACHING METHODOLOGY:Class Format: The course will involve synchronous and asynchronous lectures.Lecture Details: I will deliver all lectures live through Microsoft Teams. 3405.Title: The Economics of Addiction
3405.Description: The Economics of AddictionThis course examines addiction and related risky health behaviors using economic reasoning. It studies why some behaviors persist despite future costs, how prices and incentives affect behavior, and how information, peer influence, and regulation shape individual choices. The course begins with the main economic approaches to addiction and risky health behavior, then applies them to smoking and nicotine, alcohol, opioids, illicit drugs and fentanyl, cannabis, food and obesity, and social media and video games.The course places particular emphasis on policy. Students will study how governments use taxes, restrictions, information, advertising rules, legalization, treatment access, and harm-reduction policies to change behavior. The course will also examine how individuals, firms, and markets respond to these policies, including possible unintended effects such as substitution, avoidance, evasion, smuggling, and illicit markets. The goal is to help students use economic reasoning to understand addiction-related policy debates in a clear and disciplined way.

406.Title: Economics of Education
406.Description: The course will introduce students to some of the main topics in the area of economics of education. We will only cover education topics up to K-12 and not look at issues in higher/tertiary education or vocational training. We will present the underlying theoretical frame used in the area to set the frame for discussion. The theory will be presented in simplified form to keep the pre-requisite knowledge requirement, especially from economics, to a minimum level. Empirical papers will be used to not only present evidence from the area, but to also highlight the empirical techniques used to populate/investigate the theoretical frames. Each topic will have papers from Pakistan to not only set the local context but to present interesting local work. But each topic will also have international readings to give a good comparative setting. We will end discussion on each theme by looking at state of debate, outstanding issues, policy questions and policy options. The course will also discuss persistent issues in the literature like workplace discrimination, time poverty, different perspectives on care work, the issues faced by women-led businesses, and whether and why the overwhelming concentration of women in the informal economy should be a concern.

438.Description: This course will build upon the topics introduced initially in Econometrics I. Techniques typically employed in Microeconometric and Macroeconometric literature will be introduced and students will be given an in-depth understanding of the theory and practice of selected topics. The course will be complemented with an applied lab-based component, allowing students to practice what they have learnt in class. For most topics we cover the requisite theory and motivate the use with one or more applications. Upon successful completion, students should be well prepared to conduct rigorous empirical research and transition smoothly to graduate programs in economics and related fields. 4405.Description: This 400-level Health Economics course develops students’ ability to apply economic theory and empirical tools to understand health outcomes, public health challenges, and health care markets. Students will analyze market failures on both the demand and supply sides, interpret empirical research using causal methods, and work with health data and metrics such as DALYs and cost-effectiveness. The course is reading-intensive and emphasizes real-world applications. Discussions will draw on evidence from both developed and developing country contexts, with greater emphasis on the latter and on Pakistan wherever relevant. By the end, students will be equipped to critically assess and engage with health policies and interventions across a range of contexts

511.Title: Microeconomic Analysis
511.Description: This course provides an introduction to the content and methods of microeconomic theory, designed for the master students in economics program. The specific topics to be covered are optimization theory, producer theory, consumer theory, and choice under uncertainty. As a part of the master program, this course presumes that students have already taken undergraduate-level microeconomics courses and basic mathematics, such as multivariable calculus, linear algebra, and some basic concepts in real analysis. The course is intended students to establish systematic foundations in microeconomics theory and to be familiarized with economic methodologies so that they can use economic methods in their research

531.Title: Econometrics and Research Methodology I
531.Description: The course will provide an understanding of basic econometric theory at the graduate level, and allow students an opportunity to use these tools through applications. The workhorses will be the classical linear regression and multiple regression models. Issues in hypothesis testing, specification, non-linearity and functional forms, heteroscedasticity, autocorrelation, models for panel data, systems of regression analysis, time series models, simultaneous equations models, discrete dependent variables, and nonlinear regression models will be studied. Some large sample and asymptotic results in the context of these models will be discussed. The students are expected to be familiar with matrix algebra, calculus and statistics at the elementary level

212.Title: Sociology of Education
212.Description: The education system is both a source of perpetuating socio-economic inequalities, and a tool for challenging the status quo. Educational institutions, especially schools are an integral part of the socialization process, preparing the next generation to take on their role as “social” actors. The course examines how and why the education system perpetuates or challenges existing inequalities within society. It introduces students to sociological theories of education, examining the intersection between education, class, culture, gender, resistance and democracy. The first part provides a macro level analysis of education and its place within society by introducing students to grand theories of education with a particular emphasis on functionalism, pragmatism, and critical pedagogy. The second part focuses on the formalized education system, in particular the school, examining the structure and organization of the school, teaching and pedagogy, classroom inequalities, and the politics of language and curriculum. The third part explores contemporary debates on technology and AI and its role in the formal education system. The readings therefore move from a macro level analysis to the micro unit of the school, highlighting both the potential and the limitation of modern day schooling in challenging existing inequalities within society.

222.Title: The Learning Gap: Critical Issues in Educational Psychology
222.Description: "There are three things to remember about education: The first one is motivation. The second one is motivation. The third one is motivation.” - Terrell H. BellWhat makes an individual want to learn or to not learn? What makes an individual want to achieve and engage deeply in learning? What makes an individual want to study some subjects over others? What makes anyone want to do anything at all? This course covers a range of contemporary perspectives on some of the most important issues in educational psychology that offer some ways to answer these questions related to topics such as, learning styles, achievement, student goals, engagement, self-beliefs, effective learning environments and most importantly motivation . The major focus of this course is an introduction to learner engagement & motivation in the way it is defined in contemporary educational psychological theory and related research. The perspectives that are discussed are chosen because they are theoretically sound, empirically verified and have significant implications for learning and teaching. These seminal theories and perspectives serve as a foundation to an extensive empirical research base that enables students to learn about the nature of engagement, achievement & motivation in their own lives, with an emphasis on learning and educational settings.Students will be exposed to different theories of learning and what motivates individuals to learn, leading to discussions about the relationships between motivation, engagement, goals and achievement. A review of learning styles, the concept of multiple intelligences, learner attitudes, social-cognitive motivational theories and sociocultural conceptions of motivations form the backbone of the course. A significant part of this discourse dives into motivational constructs such as self-efficacy, self-determinism, expectancy and value constructs, the approach-avoidance debate, learned helplessness, attribution and achievement goal theory.The most interesting aspect of motivation that this course will reveal is that few individuals really understand their own motives and are hence unable to systematically drive themselves towards effective goal setting and goal achievement. During this course, students will become highly self-aware about their own motives and will develop skills to become individuals who can cultivate optimal motivation in others. By the end of the course students will amass a wealth of practical and applied strategies to enhance motivation in the self and others. They will master how to use knowledge of motivation to effectively engage with their learning situations in order to achieve success and achieve their goals.Course readings will be grounded in theoretical and empirical literature related to theories of learning and motivation. Class assignments will draw heavily on interactions with students in learning environments as a way to investigate and document theoretical constructs encountered in course readings and discussions.What brings the entire theoretical discussion together at the culmination of the course is the examination of specific strategies to encourage motivation to learn through the introduction of the TARGET model.The course will conclude with several weeks devoted to examining research on interventions that target motivation, student engagement, learning and achievement"This course is being taught by "Ifrah Nadeem" in Fall Semester 2025
222.Specific Scheduling Information: Open for all Sophomore, Junior and Senior.

223.Title: Trauma-Informed Education Systems: Creating Cultures of Support and Change
223.Description: Traumatic stress changes the way we perceive and present in the world. It also impacts how our brains can assimilate and utilize information. This course will focus on understanding trauma and how it impacts students, staff, and the educational community at large, especially in the Pakistani context. Moreover, this course will equip professionals to support students who have experienced trauma and to create trauma-informed pedagogical systems that promote well-being and learning. This is a highly reflective course and introspective curiosity is encouraged. The class will be set up as a trauma-informed space in itself*. We will also explore best practices and policies of education systems that have employed a trauma-informed lens and do a historical overview of the trauma-informed movement in Education.*Although trauma-informed systems foster respect and safety, studying or discourse on some materials might be potentially triggering for some students. Mental health resources are available on campus should you experience emotional distress.

274.Title: Gender Media and Education
274.Description: This course examines the relationship between gender, media and education with a particular emphasis on learning about the impact of growing up immersed in the digital world of today. Children spend more time interacting with different media (television, music, movies, using tablets and smart phones, online and social media) than the time they spend in schools. The central question in this course is what do children learn from media, and what issues does it raise for them? In the first part of the course, we will explore popular and theoretical discourses around gender, media and education paying particular attention to how media and education shapes and is shaped by societies, economies and civic life. In the second part of the course, we will focus more closely on new media, examining the digital mediation of our social lives and its effects on individuality, identity, communication, relationships and social belonging.Learning activities in this course include lectures, screenings, presentations by guest experts, class discussions, and student presentations.

3103.Title: Educational Inequalities in South Asia
3103.Description: In this course, we will explore the complex dynamics of educational inequalities in South Asia through both theoretical and empirical lenses. We will examine what it means to be “educated” within different South Asian contexts and how various forms of inequality—whether based on gender, class, caste, ability, or geography—shape access to and experiences of education. By investigating the intersections of politics and power, we will critically assess how education systems can simultaneously challenge and reinforce these inequalities from a social justice perspective.Key questions guiding the course include:•	How is inequality understood and defined across different South Asian countries?•	In what ways do social and political factors contribute to educational disparities?•	How do gender, caste, and economic class influence educational opportunities and outcomes?Grounded in an interdisciplinary approach that draws from development studies, sociology, and anthropology, the course is particularly well-suited to students in the social sciences. It will be run as a student-led seminar, with a strong emphasis on discussion, active participation, and presentations. Engaging with the readings before each class is essential, as the course depends on collaborative dialogue and critical analysis.

315.Title: Education in the Globalized World
315.Description: Education in the globalised world places education in the current age of globalisation. It tries to understand, analyse and critique the impact of globalisation on education. The course has four main themes. The first theme allows students to understand the dialectic between the global and local in understanding global-local interlinkages of educational policies, practices, and agendas. Using the lenses of global systems theory and global culture theory, students will study both convergence (isomorphism) and divergence in the educational field. They will study several global agendas such as EFA and SDGs, the role of several global multilateral organisations, such as the World Bank, and try to see both positive and negative impacts of these transnational bodies on local educational systems. In order to bridge the gap between theory and practice- Students will also be exposed to several case studies and documentaries focusing on “glocalisation”, indigenous education and local knowledge from Pakistan and other contexts.  The second theme of course deals will the global knowledge economy. Extending the global-local debate further, this section tackles themes related to the global knowledge economy that the current era of globalisation has formed. Increased economic competition has impacted the educational field as well. In this section, students will analyse first, the linkages of education with the global economic competition and then analyse some of the standardised educational testing and assessment systems such as PISA to critique this increased educational competitiveness amongst countries. Third theme of the course acquaints students to the global norms and expectations in the educational field by introducing them to some of the global agendas such as the EFA. Students will also study the role of multilateral organizations and international aid agencies in this global-local equation. The fourth part of the course deals with global educational issues. Majorly, the themes that will be tackled here are very current and relevant for students. Course will discuss global students’ mobility and students’ problems arising from it, distance education, online education in the wake of Covid-19, multiculturalism in classrooms.  Overall, the course takes a very current outlook and student-centered approach in order to ensure that everything that is being taught provides relevance for students.This course is being taught by "Mashal Mushtaq" in Fall Semester 2025

3204.Title: Enhancing Inclusion: Exploring Autism and Intellectual Disability
3204.Description: Autism and intellectual disability are characterized by skill deficits and/or behavioral challenges that can severely hinder independent learning. Occurrence of these delays in early childhood influences school readiness and the acquisition of pre-requisites necessary to engage in formal learning, such as in school-based contexts. This course will walk students through the definitions and etiology of both disorders, the misconceptions surrounding them and the danger and appeal of fad treatments. The course will cover a range of concerns that arise for individuals with Autism and/or Intellectual Disability such as problem behavior, self-help and adaptive skill deficits, cognitive and executive function deficits, communication skills, social skills training and more. We will also look at the multidisciplinary evidence-based treatment approaches to address these concerns using cased based applications and analytical exercises. Students can expect to gain a comprehensive understanding of how what these disorders are, the effective treatment modalities used to address them in educational contexts and the relevance of this knowledge in a classroom setting to design inclusive learning environments
