321.Title: Inclusive Pedagogy: Rethinking teaching, learning and assessment
321.Description: Inclusive Pedagogy: Rethinking Teaching and Learning is an undergraduate course that delves into the pedagogical practices and strategies for fostering inclusive and equitable learning environments in any educational setting. We will take a holistic view of inclusion, encompassing various dimensions such as ability, class, race, socio-cultural diversity, socio-economic disparities, and gender. Students will examine the theoretical foundations, evidence-based practices, and transformative approaches to promote inclusiveteaching and learning.Students will also critically examine the barriers that hinder inclusive practices and explore strategies to foster an inclusive culture within the classroom and beyond. By examining international models of inclusive education, students will develop a nuanced understanding of how cultural, social, and economic factors impact educational access and quality.The course further encourages critical analysis of educational systems, policies, and practices that perpetuate inequalities. Students will explore and debate the intersectionality of identities, and the role of privilege, power dynamics, bias, and discrimination in shaping educational experiences.

352.Title: Education Policy Analysis
352.Description: Education policies are formulated, mandated, and rolled out in pursuit of goals suited to the aspirations in each social and political system. However, quite often, outcomes remain at variance with or fall short of the stated policy objectives at the point at which the rubber hits the road, i.e., classrooms and schools. Pakistan has over seven decades of history of the variance between stated education policy aspirations and subsequent outcomes. Understanding this variance requires policy analysis along such dimensions as how and who assessed and framed a ‘problem,’ attached a ‘solution’ to the problem, and gave prominence to it in the policy and political agendas and arenas. How do policy, politics, and power intersect to shape education policy? What role do ‘narratives’ play in promoting pet agendas and policy images? This course has been designed to explore these and similar questions. The course will delve deep into the discourses in the social policy purposes, processes, perspectives, and frameworks to enable the participants to explore the shaping and unfolding of education policy in specific areas. Selected policy verticals include privatization, accountability, assessment, language, leadership, and teacher development. The course will also provide opportunities to engage with prominent issues in evaluation, communication, and advocacy of education policy.
352.Specific Scheduling Information: Open for all Sophomore, Junior and Senior.

353.Title: Education and Conflict
353.Description: The relationships between armed conflict and education are complex. Education can reflect inequalities and reinforce social tensions; it can contribute to peace, stability, and community development. Research shows that in areas affected by conflict student dropout rates increase, enrolments decrease, academic achievement is low, and students suffer from stress. Historical analysis indicate that educational institutions often cannot operate during times of crisis, leading local family and teacher networks to develop informal education systems in unconventional spaces.This course examines the multidimensional and multidirectional relationships between armed conflict and education. We will use case studies from conflict affected countries, to find a link between practice and policy of education in conflict. The lectures, and discussions will focus on reconceptualising education in conflict settings as part of a broader learning environment. A combination of readings, lectures, discussions, multimedia, and guest speakers will be used to deepen our understanding of the issues in education and conflict.

359.Title: Decolonial Theories in Education
359.Description: This course explores international and comparative education through a decolonial lens to advance new perspectives in the field. Grounded in frameworks presented by Walter Mignolo, Catherine Walsh, Arturo Escobar, and Anibal Quijano (among others), students will explore coloniality in epistemology and educational praxis. The issues discussed in class will include indigenous people’s right to education and other ways of knowing —with a focus on preserving linguistic and cultural diversity of peoples across the world. Key themes include the right to education, the nature of citizenship, international and bilingual education, indigenous resistance, and decolonizing methodologies. The broader goal is to critique policy for educational access, intercultural training, cultural responsiveness, and teacher education at all educational levels in an effort to construct new epistemological possibilities.This course is being taught by "Joti Ghani" in Fall Semester 2025

412.Description: The course will introduce students to some of the main topics in the area of economics of education. We will present the underlying theoretical frame used in the area to set the frame for discussion. Each topic will have papers from Pakistan to not only set the local context but to present interesting local work. But each topic will also have international readings to give a good comparative setting. We will end discussion on each theme by looking at state of debate, outstanding issues, policy questions and policy options. 422.Title: Behavior Analysis for Effective Teaching
422.Description: The scientific study of behavior, also known as Behavior Analysis, has been used widely to improve teaching and increase learning across content areas, grade levels, and student populations, as well as manage disruptive learning behaviors. Based on a single subject approach, its technologies allow a teacher to assess, monitor and design instructional programs that cater to individual student needs, a quality that has led to its widespread use in special needs classrooms for nearly 60 years, in addition to informing teaching strategies for atypical educational settings. This course aims to equip students with key behavior analytic knowledge and strategies that allow them to effectively teach a diverse population, including students with special needs such as Autism or ADHD, regardless of class level, or the specific curriculum being taught. We examine the science of behavior, mechanisms of learning and reinforcement, functional assessment methods to understand the causes of behavior, and function-based learning tools and techniques adapted for the classroom. The course then moves towards setting behavioral objectives for academic goals, developing programs to shape desirable classroom behavior, decrease problem behavior and teach students self-management strategies. The course also presents special considerations on the ethics of punishment in an educational setting, as well as why and how to avoid it. Throughout the course, concepts are illustrated through examples of their application in a wide variety of classroom settings, from early years to college level.

512.Title: The Arts and Education
512.Description: "This course will introduce current practices of arts education, their historical and philosophical contexts and emerging directions, globally and in our region. Pakistan has a vibrant tradition of formal education in the arts since the middle of the 19th century.However, till recently, this legacy has had limited outreach and impact on the lives of children, youth and citizens outside the realm of the art world and the art academy. The arts have tremendous scope and potential to transform understanding and shift perceptions. If encountered in meaningful ways, they can elicit deep and lasting higher-order thinking in individuals and communities. In the difficult times we are seeing today, particularly with regard to equity, access, criticality and a loss of the relational aspect of life, mobilizing the arts for peace, resilience, citizenship and inclusive education has become more crucial than ever before. In this regard, based on an overview of the field, this course aims to investigate, question, interpret and problematize the arts within the context of education through curriculum building, historical analysis or a generative field inquiry using the arts as a prompt.Students will encounter course content through published research in their required and recommended readings, as well as throughvisual presentations (lecture slides, photos, short films/film excerpts) of practices, contexts and case studies of arts education by the instructor. In addition, selected guest lectures have also been scheduled with relevant practitioners from our region who will make short presentations of arts education practices in class. The course will encourage interdisciplinary thinking and ways of approaching course content based on students’ specific discipline/s so as to ensure that the content is contextually relevant to each student’s personal research trajectory as it evolves through the program. Discussions and reviews both within and outside class will helpidentify the students’ emerging interests of inquiry in the subject. To this end, but not limited to it, an important element of the course will come together in an emergent online discussion forum where students and instructors will together extend class contentinto a dynamic conversation through reflections, debates and questions, as they surface from connections between the readings and the practices shared in class. This will be an opportunity for student initiated discussions and co-learning which are expected to define the directions of their class projects."Teaching Methodology:-------------------------------Students in this course will engage with course questions through class discussions, small- group work (Ideation and Visible Thinking Routines), reflective writing, course reading responses and mini lectures. Course readings are crucial components of student learning and are therefore mandatory. Students are expected to do all assigned readings carefully and punctually prior to the class as their understanding of issues discussed in class will be based on these readings. This course will be delivered remotely through synchronous interactions via Zoom during the bi-weekly class time, and asynchronous interaction via a course Discussion Forum in which the instructor will respond to student reading reflections and other relevant content posted by both students and instructors to develop a rich discussion on the subject.Grading Breakup:-----------------------Sessional--------------Attendance and Class Participation: 10%Reading responses: 20%Discussion Forum: 20%Midterm Project----------------------Reflective Essay 20%Final Project------------------Curriculum prototype / Field study / Historiographical essay 30% (20% written component + 10% presentation)

540.Title: Leadership: The Politics of Change
540.Description: This course is about the practice of leadership. By using a diagnostic framework, students will learn to break apart the complexity inherent in adaptive challenges we face at the societal, organizational and individual levels. The first part of the course will focus on a systems-level (outside-in) understanding of stakeholders, perspectives, pressures and politics that operate in lock-step inhibiting reform. In the second part of the course, the focus will shift towards applying the same concepts at the individual-level (inside-out) to reveal the internal narratives, loyalties, histories and identities that inhibit the courage and creativity that is crucial in exercising leadership

553.Title: Politics of Education Reform
553.Description: This course aims to help students analyse educational change as a process mediated by power distributions and dynamics that involve a range of agents, their ideological positions, and their relationships. Instead of framing the importance of education in seemingly neutral normatives, this course seeks to unpack underlying values, ideas, institutional norms and domains of agentic contestation that give rise to decisions and policies affecting educational reform: how do these push and pull against, with, around each other to produce teaching and learning as we have come to recognize it in the contemporary world? The scope of this course is deliberately restricted to school education, although there is a recognition that reform happens at all levels (and in all forms) of education. Additionally, although the course draws upon theoretical frameworks and cases globally, it is designed with the Pakistani context in mind. It is taught as a selection of topics pertinent to the politics of education reform, keeping in mind that a complete coverage of all dimensions would take this course beyond the scope of an undergraduate semester at the university. The bulk of the course relates to some of the most recent scholarship and debate emerging in the areas of effective education service delivery and change. Although this course is designed to be taught in person, it can easily be taught in an online environment as well. All classes shall remain synchronous, and conducted in seminar format. This implies that students will have completed the reading for each session ahead of time, and come prepared with discussion questions and contributions. It also implies that the instructor does not deliver a traditional lecture; instead, questions are placed before the class to initiate and nudge discussion on the scheduled reading, eliciting creative and critical responses about said material from class participants.

560.Title: Research Methods in Education
560.Description: this is a foundational course that introduces students to the philosophical underpinnings of research, especially in the education sector, and takes them through introductory components of the research process. It emphasises the development of clear argument in the form of literature review/theoretical framework development and asks them to produce a collection of data collection instruments that can generate qualitative and quantitative data. A portion of the coursework is dedicated to qualitative and (to a much lesser extent) quantitative analytical approaches. All applied work in this course is based on the specific component under study, not a consolidated research project. This means students can be asked to repeat component development (such as a theoretical framework) until such time that they can meet a previously declared standard of competence.

590.Title: Observing Schools
590.Description: The field engagement component of the MPhil Educational Leadership and Management Program is designed with the intent to ensure students receive “real world” exposure to school settings as part of the program, through a series of visits over the course of two semesters. This course will run through Year 1 of the MPhil program and prepare students for the pro-seminar and practicum in the second year. The objectives of the course are: •	Introduction to diversity in the provision of education through exposure to a variety of school organizations, management systems etc. •	Acquisition of sensibility and skills for structured observation and documentation through various methods; including through field notes, interviews, classroom observations, focus group discussions, questionnaire and survey design. Exposure to diversity is necessary for understanding the breath and dynamics of Pakistan’s educational landscape. School visits in the first semester will be organized with this goal in mind. 540.Title: Leadership: The Politics of Change
540.Description: This course is about the practice of leadership, using a diagnostic framework to break apart thecomplexity of adaptive challenges we face at the societal, organizational and individual levels. Itprovides a diagnostic and strategic foundation for leadership practice. The first part of the coursewill focus on a systems-level (outside-in) understanding of stakeholders, perspectives, pressures and politics that operate in lock-step inhibiting reform. In the second part of the course, the focus will shift towards applying the same concepts at the individual-level (inside-out) to reveal theinternal narratives, loyalties, and identities that inhibit the courage and creativity that is crucialin exercising leadership.The course is a close replica of the Adaptive Leadership courses taught at Harvard Kennedy Schooland incorporates elements of the Negotiations Workshop taught at Harvard Law School.Designed for professionals from diverse backgrounds, the course builds upon the extraordinaryexperience of many of our students. The purpose of the course is to increase one’s capacity tolead with and without authority, across boundaries, and from any political or organizationalposition.Part 1: Systemic (outside-in): In a world in which most organizations, communities, and societiesface enormous adaptive pressures, the practice of leadership is critical – the practice ofmobilizing systems of people to thrive in changing and challenging times. In this course, we applytheory to practice, clarifying the relationship among key concepts – leadership, management,authority, power, influence, and followership, citizenship – to provide a practical, coherent, andclear theoretical framework. We develop both diagnostic tools for analyzing the complexity ofchange in social systems, and strategies of action, for example: using authority and powerproperly, mobilizing engagement across boundaries, generating innovation, orchestrating multiparty conflict, regulating disequilibrium, refashioning narratives to both build and depart fromhistory, and building a culture of adaptability for the long-term. In addition, we explore thechallenge of managing personally the inevitable stresses of leadership.Part 2: Individual (inside-out): To lead is to live dangerously. Although it may be exciting to thinkof leadership as inspiration, decisive action, and powerful rewards, leading requires taking risksthat can jeopardize your career and your personal life. It requires putting yourself on the line,disturbing the status quo, and working with hidden conflicts. And when people resist and pushback, there is a strong temptation to play it safe. Those who choose to lead take the risks, andsometimes get wounded and neutralized. Part 2 of this course has three parts: a) the sources andforms of danger in leadership; b) diagnostic, strategic, and tactical responses to these dangers;and c) how to stay alive, not only in your job, but in your heart and soul. Part 2 is designed tocomplement Part 1 which takes a systemic approach to diagnosis and action. It explores theindividual factors that determine success and survival.The course draws from several disciplines: Philosophy and biology provide the concepts ofparadigmatic change and adaptation. Political science and business management provideperspectives on the functions of authority. History and literature provide a rich caseload fromwhich to explore the nature of adaptive success and failure. Social psychology provides insightinto the dynamics of social systems and an approach to diagnose their productivity anddysfunctions. Music provides a language for working with the practices of inspiration, creativity,listening, partnership, and harmony (consonance, dissonance, and resolution).

590.Title: Observing Schools
590.Description: Observing Schools is a field-oriented course that is meant to expose students to the diverse landscape of school education in Pakistan so that they are better able to understand the unique challenges faced by different types of schools and the issues plaguing education policy in the country. Schools vary by type of ownership, size, the socio-economic group they cater to. There are variations also within each category in the types of curricula, modes of instruction, quality of governance and teaching.The Executive MPhil having weekend only classes, however, means that the students will not be able to freely visit SOE partner schools that operate only during weekdays. Consequently, keeping the course objective of exposing students to the diverse dynamics of the educational sector of Pakistan, EDUx 590 will be based on the dynamic principle of “Peer to Peer Learning” in order to take advantage of the accomplished and diverse professional background of the students of Observing Schools. In our cohort we have students who work in elite private schools, universities, NGO or Trust Schools, various governmental departments and services related to education and vocational schools as teachers, coordinators, principals, or researchers. This diversity of experiences and qualifications will allow us to make small groups once the semester starts that will reflect this wide range of educational roles and contexts. These small groups will comprise of 4 students, and the total number of groups can range from 8 to 10 depending on final cohort size. Our students will learn from one another by interviewing their peers in the groups and visiting their workplaces, where possible. Furthermore, these groups will meet at least once a week to have highly structured sessions where the members will discuss and critically analyze one another’s organizations and their missions and the context or constraints they operate in, while ensuring a supportive and ethical collaborative environment. We will try to facilitate visits to these office spaces or remote work environments by the group members where we can, and the general expectation will be that these visits will be timed and organized by the students among themselves during the working week.These “small group meetings” will serve as the backbone for the discussion in the scheduled Saturday classes, where the insights and findings from each subgroup will be shared with the larger class for the benefit of everyone’s learning. Observing Schools will be taking place in the latter half of the semester and will give the students an opportunity to practice skills learnt in Research Methods such as observation skills, interviews, focus groups and qualitative data analysis. The timing of the course also means that the students will have gotten to know each other, and this will facilitate the makeup of the small groups. The exact structure for small group discussions will depend on the make up of these groups and the types of organizational contexts being studied.

202.Title: Data Structures
202.Description: Data structures are abstractions for storing data in a computer system and form an essential building block in the design of efficient algorithms. The knowledge of data structures plays a central role in computer science and engineering and is highly sought-after in the technology industry. They are used in a wide variety of applications today including search engines (e.g., Google, Bing), social networking applications (e.g., Facebook, Twitter), embedded systems (e.g., cell phones, robots), and DNA analysis. This course introduces the fundamentals of data structures and aims to provide a deep understanding of how to systematically organize data in a computer system.The students will be introduced to analytical tools for comparing different data structures in terms of their time and space complexity. Finally, the course will augment student’s theoretical understanding of data structures with rigorous programming assignments, which form an essential component of the course. 203.Title: Engineering Models
203.Description: Engineering models allow Scientists and Engineers to understand systems under study by performing experiments. Differential equations have been the main tool (models) for the mathematical analysis, comprehension, design and prediction of things that change. The emergence of digital computers has provided alternative methods for the approximate analysis for both natural and man-made systems through numerical solutions. This course describes both the analytical techniques for solving first order and second order differential equations as well as describes a wide range of unrelated physical phenomenon that can be modelled through them. 453.Title: Power System Protection and Stability
453.Description: Power system protection is an integral part of any electric power system. It becomes very important during faults and abnormal operating conditions. The power equipment needs protection against short circuits, lightning strikes, failure due to insulation deterioration, inadvertent contingencies, and improper operation of the power systems. The damage to the expensive equipment results in significant economic loss. The power outage translates into severe damage to the national economy due to production disruption. Frequent outages affect people's daily routines. A carefully applied protective relaying scheme limits the power disruption to a minimum number of users and ensures the unaffected operation of the rest of the power system in the event of a fault. This course is intended to provide a deep understanding of the fundamentals of power system protection and stability. The short-circuit calculations for symmetrical and unsymmetrical faults will be covered. The symmetrical components and sequence networks of various power elements will be described. Different protective relaying schemes related to overcurrent protection, directional overcurrent protection, distance protection, and differential protection will be discussed. The application of these relays in the protection of transmission lines, transformers, busbars, and generators will be explored. The methods to select the appropriate current transformer and voltage transformer will be described. The operating principle of switchgear, such as fuses and circuit breakers, will be explained. An overview of steady-state and transient stability studies will be provided.

515.Title: Applied Probability
515.Description: This is an intermediate level course focusing on the application of probability theory to science and engineering disciplines.The first portion of the course reviews the basic probability theory with some examples chosen from science and engineering. Laterportion of the course deals with moderately advanced topics that signify the use of probability theory in these disciplines.The topics covered in the course should help the students building a background for understanding and conducting research incomputer and data sciences, estimation and learning, and other more general engineering problems. In particular, we will discussrandom variables and expectations, joint and conditional distributions, random processes, queueing systems and Markov chains,confidence intervals, and prediction/learning/estimation theory.One important application area we will cover in the course is queueing theory.Why queuing theory? Any system (e.g., a web server, a customer service center) that has finite capacity and provides a servicecan potentially be modeled using queuing theory, which provides us with tools to predict system performance as well as designsystems that achieve high performance. For example, using queuing theory we can answer questions such as “What is the averagedelay experienced by requests arriving at a web server?” and “Given demand and a size of a given hospital, how many doctorsshould be hired to ensure that the no patient waits for longer than 10mins with high, say 98 percent, probability?”).We will also provide a brief introduction to machine learning, another important application area that has gained recent popularity.Why machine learning? Computers are increasingly being used as data analysis tools to obtain insights from the enormous amountsof data that is being collected in a variety of fields (now referred to as “big data”). Probability theory is now used as one of thekey methods for designing new algorithms to model such data, allowing, for example, a computer to make predictions aboutuncertain or new events. A use case would be to predict the weather tomorrow given weather data for past 10 years.A key goal of this course is to act as a bridge between the theoretical foundations of probability and its applications.

517.Title: Deep Learning
517.Description: Deep Learning is a hierarchical learning methodology based on artificial neural networks which are algorithms inspired by the structure and function of the brain. It has applications in wide-range of industries these days such as face-recognisers working at massive scales, robotics, speech translation, text analysis, improving customer experience, autonomous vehicles etc. In this course we will take a “hands-on approach” and start will implementation of basic building blocks such as training a simple perceptron and move to design and train a deep convolution neural network. Course will concentrate in developing both mathematical knowledge and implementation capabilities. The implementations will be python based using TensorFlow and Keras. After establishing our foundation in convolutional neural networks we will start looking into applications of deep learning in both spatial as well as time-series data and explore various network architectures suited for each. The objective is to help you build a career in AI and Machine learning, to make you comfortable enough that you can understand various learning problems and develop your own deep learning based solutions.
517.Specific Scheduling Information: Open for EE-MS, DES-MS, PESG-MS and EE-PHD during Add/Drop period.

520.Title: Computer Architecture
520.Description: This course extends the concepts of computer organization and uniprocessor architecture to more advanced topics. These topics include advanced pipelining, instruction level parallelism (ILP), dynamic scheduling, thread level parallelism (TLP), multi-processors, memory systems, storages and I/O devices. The course provides the students with current trends and future insight to modern computer architecture design.

5204.Title: Applied Cryptography
5204.Description: This course explores the theory, design, and implementation of modern cryptographic systems used to secure information in real-world applications. Beginning with foundational concepts such as modular arithmetic, historical ciphers, and number theory, the course advances through the design and analysis of stream ciphers, block ciphers (including AES), and public-key cryptographic algorithms like RSA and Diffie-Hellman. Students will explore cryptographic primitives and protocols—such as digital signatures, hash functions, and message authentication codes—while also analyzing system-level threats, including implementation attacks and man-in-the-middle vulnerabilities. Real-world use cases are explored in depth, including Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) security and the protection of implantable medical devices against battery depletion and other attacks. The course concludes with student-led presentations on advanced topics such as elliptic curve and post-quantum cryptography, providing a comprehensive understanding of cryptography in both theory and practice.

532.Title: Opto-Electronic Devices

In this course aphysical level description of variety of optoelectronic components will be discussed followed by comprehensive mathematical models of thedevices. The applications and limitations of various optoelectronic devices will also be covered. 5502.Title: Local Solutions for Energy Access
5502.Description: In this Master's level course, students will learn through a systems thinking approach. We'll introduce key actors and stakeholders in the local and regional energy access landscape, all in pursuit of Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7). Throughout the course, we will use real-life case studies, reports, and data analysis, and highlight both best and worst practices in global, regional, national, and local energy solutions to enhance their understanding. "The purpose of the ""Local Energy Access Course"" is to empower participants with knowledge and skills related to energy access at the local level, with a specific focus on Pakistan. The course aims to:1. Comprehensive Understanding: Provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the DRE sector, including Mini- and Micro-grids, standalone solar systems, grid integration and load considerations.2. Problem Solving for SDG7: Equip students with skills to assess DRE challenges and propose solutions in alignment with SDG7.3. Exploration of Options: Introduce various distributed generation options, from standalone solar home systems to micro-grids, while addressing drivers and barriers.4. Sustainability Focus: Promote sustainability by integrating energy efficiency, sustainable energy practices, and environmental considerations.5. Holistic Expertise: Enable students to analyze and contribute to localized and regional DRE solutions, utilizing the latest tools and data while opening up career and entrepreneurial opportunities.

555.Title: Renewable Energy Systems
555.Description: This course would review the renewable sources and their need in world energy scenario. Energy harvesting through wind and PV would be focused in this course. This course will encapsulate PV systems in detail from design of a solar cell to standalone and grid tied PV systems. Costing of renewable and hybrid systems will also be focused in this course.  The course also includes a research project in which students would be required to do a detailed literature survey and/or analysis of a known finding. Profiling of PV cells, modeling of systems and presentation of a potential PV application or detailed review of some applications in Pakistan scenario is also acceptable. Original research is encouraged however a simulation based known result would also be acceptable.

559.Title: Power System Protection and Stability
559.Description: Power system protection is an integral part of any electric power system. It becomes very important during faults and abnormal operating conditions. The power equipment needs protection against short circuits, lightning strikes, failure due to insulation deterioration, inadvertent contingencies, and improper operation of the power systems. The damage to the expensive equipment results in significant economic loss. The power outage translates into severe damage to the national economy due to production disruption. Frequent outages affect people's daily routines. A carefully applied protective relaying scheme limits the power disruption to a minimum number of users and ensures the unaffected operation of the rest of the power system in the event of a fault. This course is intended to provide a deep understanding of the fundamentals of power system protection and stability. The short-circuit calculations for symmetrical and unsymmetrical faults will be covered. The symmetrical components and sequence networks of various power elements will be described. Different protective relaying schemes related to overcurrent protection, directional overcurrent protection, distance protection, and differential protection will be discussed. The application of these relays in the protection of transmission lines, transformers, busbars, and generators will be explored. The methods to select the appropriate current transformer and voltage transformer will be described. The operating principle of switchgear, such as fuses and circuit breakers, will be explained. An overview of steady-state and transient stability studies will be provided.

567.Title: Multi-agent Systems
567.Description: "The course is about algorithmic game theory and its applications in engineering, economics, and social domains. Game theory is the study of interacting decision makers where each decision maker is acting in a selfish manner. In engineering applications, the decision makers can be robots or other computing machines that are required to achieve some desired global objective. In economics applications, the decision makers can be firms that are competing in a market for their own profit maximization. In social domain, the players can be humans interacting in societal situations like traffic or social good applications.The course will cover the basic framework for strategic games and its various manifestations. Topics include matrix games, extensive form games, mixed strategies, repeated games, Bayesian games, and cooperative games. The course will continue with an application of game theory as a design tool for multiagent systems, i.e., systems that consist of a collection of programmable decision-making components. Game theory as a design tool has applications in diverse domains like online advertisements and auctions, modeling of social phenomena, distributed optimization, resource allocation, throughput maximization in computer networks, and demand management in smart grids."

5812.Title: Introduction to Blockchain: Technology and Applications
5812.Description: This course focuses on the foundational technologies behind blockchain. We will cover the concepts of distributed ledger, consensus mechanisms, authentication techniques, and relevant protocols. The course will provide case studies of blockchain applications such as cryptocurrencies, supply chain management, and B2B/B2C/C2C scenarios. The course will also provide hands-on experience with building and deploying smart contracts.

585.Title: Communication Systems
585.Description: This course provides an overview of information communication systems. Topics include analog and digital modulation in baseband and passband. We also provide coverage of sampling and quantization techniques. In this course, system design is given primary importance by using examples from practical systems. This is supported by allied labs and simulations.

5013.Title: Understanding Financial Accounting: Making More Authoritative Decisions
5013.Description: Accounting is the universal language of business. Sound accounting principles are important for shaping capital markets. Financial Accounting is the process that culminates in the preparation of financial reports on the enterprise for use by both internal and external parties. Users of these financial reports include investors, creditors, managers, unions, and government agencies. This course introduces the concepts and issues of financial accounting with an emphasis on the interpretation of financial statements and how financial statement data can be used to assess and manage value creation activities. It takes a broad view of financial accounting and reporting encompassing virtually any external information or incentive system. This course will help students to understand what accounting can do for managers, the decision-maker, and how accounting policy choice affects decisions. Students will be exposed to the methodology and practice of accounting need to critically examine the broader implications of financial accounting for the fair and efficient working of our economy. The objective is to give the students an understanding of current financial accounting and reporting environment, taking into account the diverse interests of both external users and management. A key aspect of the course is a group presentation on the analysis of the annual reports of a sample of firms in a selected industry.

5022.Title: Corporate Finance
5022.Description: Finance for Managers is a first course in finance for Executive MBAs. This course is divided into three modules:• Cost of Capital• Capital Structure Decisions• Mergers & AcquisitionsTo provide a more solid understanding in of the more advanced concepts of finance including cost of capital, capital structure, financial institutions and markets, firm valuation, financing options, and introduction to derivatives.To enhance managers understanding of finance as applied economics within the business context with value creation as its central objective.To develop managers competency in the analysis and valuation of financial and real assets including assessment of financial risk and to highlight the role of finance function within financial markets.

5041.Title: Marketing Management
5041.Description: This is the first course in marketing and, as a result, it aims at developing a solid understanding of the basic terminologies, concepts, tools, and frameworks in marketing management. A broad range of marketing issues in a variety of consumer, industrial, and service setting is covered. Among the topics discussed in the course are consumer and industrial buying behavior, market segmentation, product positioning, elements of the marketing mix (such as, product policy, pricing strategy, integrated marketing communications, SFM and channel strategies), break-even analysis and marketing research techniques.This course is taught primarily by the case method. Hence, in addition to learning and applying the concepts and knowledge in the domain of marketing, students are expected to improve upon their attitudes, and analytical, inter-personal, communication, and decision-making skills. These skills and attitudes are enhanced by regular practice throughout the course. Various concepts, attitudes and skills are introduced repeatedly in varying contexts so as to deepen the understanding of these concepts, strengthen the attitudes, and sharpen the skills.

5063.Title: Decision Analytics
5063.Description: This course covers both quantitative and qualitative decision making. The first half of the course primarily covers quantitative decision making covering several statistical tools including testing of hypothesis, multiple regression, logistic regression time series forecasting.Second half of the course covers primarily qualitative decision making which includes decision analysis, problem solving methodology and team decision making insights.This Course is primarily taught by case method, which allows to students not only apply a tool but also understand its management application in the context of the case.

5211.Title: Business Law
5211.Description: This course provides a conceptual and practical understanding of fundamental legal concepts, principles, and frameworks relevant to the business environment. It introduces business managers to the paradigm of legal risk management in a business entity by making sense of the interaction of laws, legal institutions, and legal decisions with a business. It aims to equip business managers with the knowledge, skills, and an overall strategic mindset that will enable them to effectively manage legal risks while making better business decisions.This course introduces students to a broad array of laws; this includes the law of companies, partnerships, contracts, corporate finance, labor, property, intellectual property, and competition. It also provides an overview of certain regulatory frameworks and institutions (Competition Commission of Pakistan and the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan) and dispute resolution mechanisms. Throughout, the focus of this course is to supplements the discussion of core legal concepts with practical knowledge about legal risks and the strategies that can be used (and have been used previously by business leaders) in order to eliminate risks and sustain a competitive advantage.

6071.Title: Venture Creation
6071.Description: The first half of the course builds on the ideas and concepts covered in accounting, marketing, OB, finance, statistical analysis and modeling courses and provides an integrative perspective on management challenges and opportunities for entrepreneurs. It takes a general management perspective and helps students understand the importance of new venture/project creation in any organization for achieving competitiveness.The course is intended for individuals interested in understanding the entrepreneurial process. It is designed to provide the participant with tools and techniques to help in the growth and development of an idea; to develop the skills to think effectively about markets and strategies and to critically analyze the functional areas of business.Individuals will learn the detailed process of creating, and evaluating a new business. The course comprises the following main modules:a) Opportunity Recognition: Turning problems into business venturesb) Business Plan Writing: How to convince other about the feasibility of your planc) Marketing: Building your brandd) Managing startups: How to build a team with a common visione) Legal Issuesf) Finance Essentials for EntrepreneursThe second half of the course focuses on Corporate entrepreneurship and harnesses the business organization’s pursuit of sustainable profitable growth by employing its entrepreneurial skills into a competitive advantage. In a resource-limited business environment, the CE process can facilitate the firm’s efforts to innovate and manage business uncertainties. The major thrust of this course is to enable EMBA students to develop the entrepreneurial spirit within the workplace and engender an atmosphere of innovation to prosper.

1000.Description: This course serves as a general introduction to English literature, providing a survey of the development of literature in English from pre-modern times through to the present day. The course will analyze diverse texts including novels, short stories, and poetry to develop students’ critical faculties. Students will practice their ability to present discussion of course texts and they will assemble a glossary of critical terminology for the study of English literature. The course is designed to give students a solid grounding in some of the key works of English literature over the centuries and develop the critical tools they will require for more advanced literary studies in English.

2402.Title: Comics Scholarship and Graphic Narrative
2402.Description: This course will introduce students to the study of comics and graphic narrative, with a particular focus on the formal elements that differentiate comics from other forms of literature, such as the panel and the gutter. Students will engage critically with some of the principal works of comics scholarship while working through a reading list that looks at mainstream comics from the US and UK, as well as graphic memoir and comics journalism from around the world. Through these texts, students will explore and analyze representations of coloniality and indigeneity, racial, gender, and sexual identity, and the representation of otherness in graphic narrative.

Divided intovarious categories, the course attempts to teach students how writers use various craftand narrative techniques to deliver authentic, moving, and poignant stories about thehuman experience. 3211.Title: ‘Ring Shout’: The Slave Narrative and Its Legacy
3211.Description: "African-American slave narratives are crucial in understanding the contemporary debates around race and gender in America. Despite the abolition of slavery in the 13th amendment (1865) to the United States constitution, its conspicuous presence in the literary, cultural and political landscape of the US demonstrates its continuing importance. The slave narratives chronicle the physical, sexual, and emotional trauma caused by enslavement; this course will trace the historical development and evolution of such stories, as well as the journey towards personhood that they illustrate. We will also consider the role of gender, analysing the differing experiences of slavery for African-American men and women, and explore how gendered history impacts upon present-day debates around race. Using autobiography, fiction, poetry, cinema and literature, the course will provide a deep and broad understanding of slave narratives and their contemporary relevance and importance."

3254.Title: Whale of a Tale: 19th Century American Novel
3254.Description: "As literary pioneers, nineteenth century American writers broke away from narrative traditions, devised alternative ways of apprehending the world and produced unique works that explored the complexities of American existence. Tracing the trajectory of prose narrative, this course will be based on an in-depth study of the American novel in terms of genre, content and technique. Through a focus on the social, political and discursive contexts of literaryproduction, we will explore how nineteenth century writers delineate issues of identity, fate, slavery, morality, gender and class. Our readings will also explore to what extent the contradictory conceptions of individualism within the heteroglossic American novel internalize cultural regulation, reveal anxieties about self-determination, serve as a means of self-awareness, camouflage subversive intent and strategically promote sociopolitical reform"

4812.Title: Contagion: Text as Pathogen
4812.Description: This course will consider literary representations of language and text as forms of disease, violence, compulsion, and harm. Beginning from Burroughs’ observation that “the word is now a virus”, students will engage with a constellation of novels, short stories, and poetry that explore and extrapolate from the premise of the pathogenic text. Alongside these primary texts, students will be asked to consider a range of theoretical readings that offer models for thinking about the infection that text represents. Students will produce analysis that theorizes how the figure of language as malignancy in these texts has consequences for the act of interpretation, the ethics of text, and for reading and writing in general. Classes will lean towards a seminar model rather than lecture, therefore all students will be expected to contribute to discussion.

102.Title: Introduction to Environmental Studies
102.Description: Our environment is a product of complex mutually dependent interactions in which humans play an increasingly significant role. This course adopts an interdisciplinary approach to introduce key environmental concepts, challenges and approaches employed to address pertinent issues. The aim is to explore theories and processes that inform environmental debates, activism and policy-making across geographic regions and cultures. The first part of this course aims to develop an understanding of fundamental environmental principles and processes. It focuses on what the environment is and how human interactions with the eco-system shape the environment we live in. The second part of this course discusses critical environmental challenges faced today. These include but are not limited to: climate change and global warming, food (in)security, pollution, species extinction and water scarcity. These issues are studied in the context of world population trends and urbanization, energy consumption and the impact on climate, fragility of biodiversity and the search for sustainable development. The remainder of this course critically deliberates various approaches and strategies employed to address environmental challenges. It aims to foster ways of critically and constructively thinking about the future we may inhabit.

210.Title: Methods in Environmental Studies
210.Description: Every form of human action from an individual level to large-scale corporate actions or government interventions and development initiatives incur an environmental impact. Due to this it is important for environmentalists and others to assess the environmental impact of each action on the immediate and wider environment around them. This course will enable students to understand the existence and potential of environmental risks and issues and analyze these by undergoing research and pragmatic experiential learning. Students will be required to develop research projects addressing environmental concerns in Pakistan. Alongside traditional research methods, students will also be introduced to environmental photography, environmental impact assessment and geospatial mapping. The course will be divided into the following parts:1. Ask Environmental questionsStudents will learn the ability to formulate environmental research questions.2. 236.Title: Disasters and Society
236.Description: Current trends of increasing urbanization, the reality of climate change, threats of industrial and biological hazards, have made disasters commonplace. But there is nothing ordinary about disasters. Disasters are stress-inducing, complex events that are difficult to manage and recover from. This course introduces students to the field of disaster studies and disaster theory utilizing an interdisciplinary and a multi-disciplinary approach. The first part of the course discusses what disasters are and why they need to be studied. It provides an overview and comparison between ancient and modern disasters emphasizing the intersection between the human system and the environment. During this course disasters are discussed and framed both as highly complex events to manage, and as opportunities to learn lessons and mitigate future catastrophic events. A major part of the course introduces students to the sociological aspects of disasters: Are disasters socially constructed or are they natural? How do disasters impact the social fabric of communities? How does the society respond to the disaster? Students are introduced to key concepts in disaster studies such as risk, vulnerability and resiliency and they are challenged to think about why some communities cope and recover better than others during and after disasters. Disaster models, theories and philosophical approaches, along with myths and fallacies regarding disasters are also studied. In the context of understanding disasters, political and developmental perspectives are also introduced. The final section of the course explores the current strategies for disaster management in Pakistan.

322.Title: Environmental Governance
322.Description: Our times are marred with the colossal challenges of capping global warming, creating a net-zero world, moving towards green initiatives for sustainability and diversifying energy sources to inhibit an impending existential crisis. Better governance and policies are required to address these challenges. While it is easy to blame government inaction for these mounting environmental woes, it is not the government alone that can deliver and tackle the crisis head on. The solutions lie in a collective and collaborative multi-level (global, regional, national and local) and cross-sectoral (state and non-state stakeholders) process not only generating urgency for action but creating effective structures and policies to implement sustainable actions and innovations. During this course students will develop research projects that seek ways to transform and improve Pakistan’s environmental governance system towards a more resilient, climate-smart and sustainable system that tackles our myriad environmental problems.

336.Title: The Politics of Resources
336.Description: The Politics of ResourcesFrom Gulf oil to Indonesian timber, African blood diamonds to Sui gas, natural resources and the conflict that surrounds their control and commodification have been major sources of contention in the modern world. This course explores the historical causes and consequences of this strife, spanning all continents and employing the methods of diverse disciplines in the social sciences. The empirical scope of the course is broad, with primary data and textual materials as well as secondary readings related to case studies ranging from colonial India and the Americas to contemporary Africa and East Asia. The course begins with three weeks of introductory work to familiarise students with the conceptual frameworks and methodologies employed, and to engage them in thinking about nature and the environment as a political and sociological issue. The remainder of the course is thematically focused and structured around the distinct histories of resources themselves – land, water, oil, gas, timber, rubber, uranium, precious metals and stones. In comparing global histories of resource-commodification and conflict across time and space, we relate the physical properties of resources and technological processes involved in extraction, transport, marketization and usage to political, cultural, economic and environmental problems. These include transitions to capitalism and colonial resource regimes as well as more recent neoliberal drives to comodify ever more of the world’s natural resources. Wherever possible, case studies from Pakistan will be used to illuminate concepts and concerns. Drawing upon classical and more recent writings from across the social sciences and environmental humanities, we question the wisdom of interpretations that explain all conflict as flowing from scarcity. We also interrogate technocratic discourses about the global South’s ‘resource-curse’. Refusing simple answers to age-old questions (e.g. why does the abundance of resources rarely benefit the local communities in which they are ‘discovered’?), this course invites participants to consider the profound implications of resource-politics for regions, nations and communities in the modern period.

100.Title: Principles of Finance
100.Description: Firms invest in real assets such as plant and equipment (the Investment decision) and raise money via personal funds, stocks, bonds or bank loans (the Financing decision). Broadly speaking, Financial Management is about how this Investment and Financing decisions should be made. This course explores the first part of Financial Management and introduces the framework, tools and techniques for making Investment decisions. Specifically, we will cover Valuation, Capital Budgeting, Modern Portfolio Theory and Equilibrium Risk-Return Relationship. This is an introductory course in Finance and the first in a series of required Finance core courses for the B.Sc. Accounting & Finance degree. This course together with the next course, Intermediate Finance, completes an introduction to modern theory of Corporate Finance. The final required course in the sequence, Applied Corporate Finance, introduces advanced topics and explores certain topics in depth

200.Title: Intermediate Finance
200.Description: This course addresses major decision making areas of corporate finance within the framework of finance theory and practices. It complements and supplements concepts covered in Principles of Finance. Some of the concepts previously covered are refreshed with broader perspective and more rigorous analysis to provide solid grounding in time value of money, project analysis, and asset pricing. Portfolio theory and risk-return tradeoff implications for corporate finance decisions are examined in-depth. The course focuses on investment and financing decisions. Capital investments are also evaluated under conditions of uncertainty and risk. Financing decisions are examined through cost of capital, capital structure theory, and dividend policy. Valuation of securities integrates the impact of both investment and financing decisions. Other topics covered include review of derivative instruments, valuation of options including convertible securities, insights from option pricing framework for investment and financing decisions, and usage of derivatives for risk management and hedging exposure

353.Description: An introductory course in the analysis of investments and portfolio management. 400.Description: Applied Corporate Finance is a case-based course in intermediate level finance. 453.Title: Financial Derivatives
453.Description: The course is designed to provide an introduction, evaluation and pricing of the most important financial derivative instruments, namely forwards, futures, options and swaps. The course equips students with essential tools to be applied to value these derivatives and hedging the associated financial market exposures. The course emphasizes the importance of the general principal of pricing derivatives using no arbitrage arguments. Furthermore, the course also introduces the principal models that underpin modern financial theory and practice- the Black Scholes model and its generalization. The course also examines the pricing of options, their uses and their risk characteristics. The group/individual assignment (projects) also help students to understand the basics behind actual trading in futures by taking positions in a futures market and keeping margin accounts. The core tools that students would extensively use in this course are ratio, horizontal, vertical, YOY analyses to see how different aspects of a firm’s finances are linked with the different business strategies and how they could affect the overall business model.The second module of the course will lay the foundations of finance with an emphasis on strategic decisions corporate managers are supposed to make. 210.Title: Introduction to Gender and Sexuality Studies
210.Description: This course will be an in-depth examination of selected topics related to sexuality, the gendered body, and cultural representations and constructions of gender. Building on knowledge and experiences provided by the quoted material, we will focus on various ways to answer the following key questions: How do we understand the sexed and gendered body in contemporary society? In what ways do heteronormative ideologies, the imposition of the gender binary, and institutionalized sexism and its intersection with other marginalized identity signifiers affect our understanding of what it means to be a woman? To be a man? To be gender fluid? To be “masculine” or “feminine?” To be gay, straight, bisexual, asexual, queer? What are possible strategies and sites of resistance to these discourses?

212.Title: Women's Lives Across Cultures
212.Description: This course focuses on contemporary women’s lives in different economic and cultural settings. It examines their common experiences and some of the global processes which link them. The assigned readings and films this term deal with women living in the Sudan, Mali, Nicaragua, the U.S., China, India, France, Thailand, Pakistan, Papa New Guinea, Afghanistan, Korea, Lebanon, and Japan, as well as women who are displaced around the world.During the term we will examine some of the typical roles women play in society; the cultural rationales and structural conditions behind practices like female circumcision and women’s acceptance of and resistance to such practices; the globalization of work, sex, and ideas of female beauty; the influence different forms of social organization have on women’s lives; media images of women; and women’s social activism and development work on behalf of women. We will also spend a significant portion of the course critically deconstructing powder dynamics within the feminist movement, examining the impacts of colonization, neoimperialism, and neoliberal on contemporary feminisms, as well as the significant contributions of black, postcolonial, and indigenous feminists towards gender, sexuality, and race-based rights.As anthropologists we will be striving to acquire an insider’s perspective, but we will also examine the opinions of outsiders who typically view other women’s lives through the filter of their own culture. We will be reading about and watching films which show both women’s victimization as well as their agency and collective efforts to create better lives for themselves and for their societies and future generations.

315.Title: Masculinities
315.Description: This course provides students with an introduction to the field of masculinity studies—an area that has, until recently, received little attention in gender studies as a whole and in the Global South in particular. While earlier studies of gender focused particularly on women, there is an increasing awareness of the importance of understanding and deconstructing masculinities as a means of understanding gendered workings of power. Hence, this course will provide an overview of theories related to the social construction of masculinities historically and in diverse contexts. This is an interdisciplinary course, but emphasis is placed on sociological and anthropological approaches to the study of masculinities (as opposed to biological or psychological approaches).

3603.Title: Ethics of Romantic Love
3603.Description: This course takes an interdisciplinary approach towards exploring ethical problems in the context of romantic relationships as well as the feelings, thoughts, and actions that precede and succeed them. It is broadly divided in four modules that explore the lifecycle of romantic love through concepts such as morality, patriarchy, modernity, coloniality, capitalism, difference, violation, rationality, and temporality. The course shifts between primarily philosophical and anthropological texts each week with the goal of introducing you to historical and contemporary theories and practices of romantic ethics. The ethnographic studies assigned are mostly drawn from Muslim-majority contexts in order to limit the scope of the course and for juxtaposing and contextualizing Islamic ethics of romance in broader discourses on the same. Assigned readings – primarily peer reviewed journal articles and book chapters – will be supplemented during class with media examples such as clips from TV shows and feature films, documentaries, songs, poems, op-eds, podcasts, educational videos, magazine articles, and interviews. Course assignments will hone your critical thinking, reading, writing, speaking, and listening skills separately and together with opportunities for you to explore, develop, and share your interests and experiences with your peers. Readings and lectures are designed to accommodate students from diverse disciplines and with no prior academic training on the course topics.

414.Title: Sex and the State
414.Description: Just how political is the personal? Is the government really in your bedroom, how did they getthere, and should they stay? How come all conversations about gender feel like conversations aboutthe nation’s honor? Join us this semester to examine the critical role that sex and sexuality have playedin the development of the modern nation-state, as well as how the emergence of political modernityhas transformed our understanding of sex and sexuality in fundamental ways.This reading and writing intensive course will be rooted in anthropological concepts andmethods, while traversing widely across ethnography, critical theory, and history. Thinking through anon-exhaustive cross-section of global debates, including hijab laws, abortion politics, and imperialhomonationalism, we will interrogate the entanglements of gender, religion, nation, and colonialpower. In tandem with ethnographic deep-dives, we will read Lauren Berlant, Judith Butler, VeenaDas, Michel Foucault, Saba Mahmood, Jasbir Puar, Joan W. Scott, and other scholars.

100.Title: Introduction to Historical Studies
100.Description: One of the major purposes of this course is to give students a more nuanced account of history, the complexities of theoretical approaches impacting the writing of history, and how an analytically rigorous framework employed for the past can help us understand our societies than a simple retelling of war, dynastic charts, and chronology of events. The study of history requires an understanding of how historians approach the past, draw upon various kinds of evidence to reconstruct the past events, and weave them into a narrative in a cohesive manner. For an introductory level course on how to 'do' history, we must understand the constituent elements of all the processes and terms involved in the understanding of the past as history and the historians' methods whereby the past is cohered into an academic discipline – an account that can be used for different purposes and invoked for a range of academic or political purposes. All these debates about the facticity of what has happened and the evidence required to reconstruct a narrative indicate complex academic arguments about history's nature as a discipline, a praxis, and politics.In this course, my approach is to introduce students to a range of theoretical issues focusing on different aspects of thinking about the past, writing history, and reading texts that inform our understandings about the past and their academic reproduction in history.

2304.Title: The Making of the Islamic world
2304.Description: What did it mean to belong to the Islamic world, and who decided that? How was political authority established after the Prophet, and what made it legitimate? How did a loose community become an empire, and how was that empire governed across vast distances? What did everyday life look like in cities such as Baghdad, and how were these worlds connected through trade, travel, and networks of knowledge? And how do we know any of this—what kinds of sources do historians use, and how should they be read?This course explores these questions through the emergence of Islam and the formation of an Islamic imperium between the seventh and thirteenth centuries, with a focus on the Middle Eastern heartlands. Rather than tracing rulers and dynasties, it examines how political authority, social and economic life, and cultural production took shape across changing geographies. Drawing on primary sources, the course invites students to reconstruct this world and to think critically about how the “Islamic” is defined and studied.

3204.Title: The Past is a Foreign Country: Memory, Myth and Historical Storytelling
3204.Description: Modern historical consciousness begins with a strange and unsettling realization: the past is not simply earlier—it is fundamentally different. To think historically is to recognize that people once lived inside worlds of meaning that no longer fully translate into our own. Their assumptions, emotions, moral orders, and political imaginations do not sit quietly behind us as ‘background’; they resist us, flicker at the edges of understanding, and occasionally refuse to make sense at all. The past, in this sense, is not a record—it is an encounter with alterity.And yet, we never meet the past directly. We inherit it through stories.This course takes these conditions seriously and turns them into questions. How is the past made to feel foreign in the first place—and through what narrative strategies is that distance sustained or softened? When does storytelling bring us closer to the past, and when does it sharpen its strangeness? What happens when fiction, myth, and archive begin to speak in the same voice? Can the past ever be fully translated, or does something always remain resistant? And finally, what does it mean not to overcome the past’s foreignness, but to learn how to think with it?Bridging history and literary studies, in this course we shall examine these questions through a small selection of works—a combination of chronicle, myth, colonial text, fiction, and film—where storytelling becomes a mode of historical thinking. With a South Asian emphasis the course will explore how myth, memory, and storytelling have long coexisted and competed in our part of the world. Works like Rajatarangini and Padmavat reveal earlier narrative traditions in which history, legend and literary imagination are inseparable. In the modern period, this entanglement intensifies; Anandamath by Bankim Chandra demonstrates how the historical novel can turn the past into a charged instrument of nationalist imagination, collective identity and political aspiration.Similarly, around sites such as the Somnath temple, competing narratives of origin, conquest, and loss circulate across historiography, politics, and fiction. Here, the past fractures into irreconcilable stories: the same figure appears, by turns, as founder, invader, liberator, or symbol. In Sita Betrayed, Qurratulain Hyder reworks epic memory through fiction, unsettling inherited mythologies and revealing how gender and historical consciousness are continually rewritten through narrative form.In its final movement, the course turns to visual culture through artwork and a museum visit, where paintings—silent in themselves—acquire meaning only within narrative frames. Across these various encounters, students learn not to resolve the past’s foreignness, but to inhabit it—long enough to see that the past does not wait to be found. It takes shape only in the telling, and in every telling, it is made again—and made otherwise.

3215.Title: Imperialism and its Discontents in South Asia
3215.Description: What did British imperialism make of South Asia? And what did South Asia make of British imperialism?Beginning with the consolidation of the British imperium in the eighteenth century and ending with the violence of Partition and independence, this course traces how empire reshaped law, knowledge, caste, religion, gender, language, and even music. These transformations in turn generated the political energies, contradictions, and crises that would eventually unmake formal colonial rule.The discontents of empire then were never singular. They expressed themselves in the language of nationalism, global revolution, religious revivalism, caste emancipation, class struggle, regional identity, and feminist refusal. They also expressed themselves as collaboration, accommodation, and the strategic use of colonial institutions for ends their architects never foresaw. This course takes that plurality seriously, resisting the temptation to reduce the history of colonial South Asia to a neat and misleading binary of oppression and resistance.Throughout, students will engage with primary sources alongside historiographical debates. Because history writing, as this course will argue, shaped history itself.

3314.Title: Technology and Social Change
3314.Description: This course explores the impact of technology on the world through a longue durée perspective. Through a series of case-studies spread temporarily and geographically across the world, the course explores the role of technology in deep historical change and transformation. The course is divided into four parts. The first part focuses on the Pre-Industrial era and explores topics such as the role of the stirrup in power structures in medieval Europe, and long durée transformations in war technologies. The second-part explores the post-industrial era: the industrial revolution, the concept of the technological Anthropocene, the rise of the modern bureaucratic state, large technological systems and the military-industrial complex. The third part examines international relations: the role of technology in imperialism and the structural impacts of transport and communications. The fourth section explores technological utopias and dystopias in intellectual thought (e.g. Marx) and culture (science fiction). Assessment: regular response papers, class participation, presentation, and a final research essay. This is a reading intensive course with set readings to be completed before each class. Students are expected to already have taken reading intensive courses (at least two 200 (or higher) level HIST/ENGL/ANTHO/SOCIO courses). This course CANNOT be taken pass/fail.

372.Title: US Imperialism
372.Description: With more than 900 bases around the world, the United States maintains a global presence that outstretches any empire in history despite ostensibly being just a nation-state. Concentrated around global trade chokepoints and key sites of production and extraction, this constellation of military outposts lays the foundation for an ""imperialism of free trade"": a system in which military dominance guarantees ready access for capital to all corners of the world and the power to set the terms of participation in global markets. This course develops a precise understanding of that system, its historical origins, and the particular character of its latest and most consequential iteration under US power.We begin with the hypothesis that while there have been innumerable empires in our past, imperialism is something far rarer. Only two other powers have attempted it, the Portuguese with their enforced commercial licenses, and the British as self-appointed guardians of the free seas. Building on this legacy and taking lessons from their failures, the United States realized a distinctly anti-colonial form of imperialism, operating through de jure sovereign nation-states instead of foreign dominions. This configuration, anchored by a global network of military bases and the infrastructure of dollar supremacy, promised invisibility and with it longevity. The possibility of being everywhere without being anywhere. Lifting the cloak it claims for itself, through the course we track two inextricably related mechanisms that make its power visible: (1) coercive authority through a global military base network, arms sales, and covert operations, and (2) less overtly coercive power to shape markets and capital flows through dollar dominance, key commodity production control, international institutions, and sanction threats.Having developed a conceptual and historical map of US imperialism, in the last part of the course we reassess the short life of the Washington Consensus world. For a brief moment in the 1990s, with the fall of the Berlin Wall and China's entry into the WTO, the American order felt not just universal but permanent. That confidence did not survive the Global War on Terror, and it has not survived the rise of alternate centers of military and market power. One can already dream of obituaries. But the death of US primacy will not be the death of US imperialism. Just as colonial withdrawal only created a postcolonial world, structured by the very forces it claimed to leave behind, American retreat will leave us in a post-American order still built in its image. This course provides the empirical grounding and conceptual vocabulary to understand not only how that order was constructed but what it will leave behind.

471.Title: Civil Procedure
471.Description: "According to Sir John Salmond the Law of procedure may be defined as that branch of the law which governs the process of litigation. It is the law of actions and include all legal proceedings whether civil criminal. In Pakistan the law which governs the civil procedure is the Code of Civil Procedure (Act of 1908) which was enacted on 21st March 1908 and is a Consolidating and amending statute. The first Code of the Civil Procedure was enacted in 1859 and was amended in 1860, 1861 and 1874. The second code was enacted in 1882 which was amended in 1882, 1888, 1892, 1894 and finally in 1895. The present Code applies to all courts of Civil jurisdiction except excluded by High Court Rule and Orders and Supreme Court in its Civil Original and Appellate jurisdiction By Central Laws (Statute Reforms) Ordinance, 1960 the Code has been extended to the whole of Pakistan. The Code is primarily a procedural law though it contains substantive provisions. The Code is divided in two parts containing sections which deal with the substantive law and the second parts contains rules which govern the procedure for exercise of the rights under civil jurisdiction. The Code regulates the civil proceedings and the nature of proceedings is not necessarily dependent upon the nature of jurisdiction of the court involved and a proceeding involving the assertion of a civil right is a civil proceeding"
