220.Title: Contracts
220.Description: Private parties form private agreements; but, a contract is a legal status which comes into existence after a bargained for exchange of legal detriments, coupled with an absence of excuses towards its enforcement. This Course is designed to introduce students to the law of Contract in Pakistan. The purpose of this course is to investigate the basic and complex rules governing contractual relations in Pakistan. The course is also designed to equip students with a basic understanding of how other legal systems operate, and shall encourage students to critically analyze the rules that are applicable to the Pakistani Legal System. The course shall begin with introducing students to Contractual theory, and the rules regulating offers and acceptances. Consideration for a promise shall follow, coupled with its understanding as a requirement to create an enforceable contract as well as its evidentiary function. The course shall then highlight the issues relating to capacity to engage in contractual relationships as well as formal requirements for certain transactions. Remedies, coupled with a measure of damages in case of breach of a legally enforceable contract shall be the last part of the Course

222.Description: This course covers the modern law of torts. Tort liability imposes common law duties on parties that are not bound by contract. Since most private actions are not contracted¿for, and since common law duties are not assumed by choice or referendum, the law of torts is important to the functioning of a civilized society- it marks the boundaries of civil behavior. We will study materials from Pakistani, British, and American jurisdictions. The readings include court opinions, statutes, agency letters, scholarly articles,¿and excerpts from books. This diversity of sources reflects the myriad influences that shape the common law

303.Title: Advanced Writing from the Trial
303.Description: This course will focus on four texts featuring trials that subject the law to crisis and re-evaluation, and address its unacknowledged histories and dialectical relationship with social processes. We will read two fictions along with one memoir and one work of reportage. We will devote generous time to unpacking each one of our four texts, with the aid of readings drawn from a plurality of disciplines. Students will be asked to analyse the connections between the legal, social, literary and philosophical questions embedded in them, and to think about their impact on legal and social knowledge more generally. In E. M. Forster’s A Passage to India (1924) and J.M. Coetzee’s Disgrace (1999) we shall grapple with the dynamics of legal process in contexts of domination and dispossession, settler-colonialism, gendered violence, and racial power. A detailed reading of philosopher Hannah Arendt’s landmark work of reportage Eichmann in Jerusalem(1964) will allow students to reassess the relevance of the trial of Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann for understanding the legal and political strategies of the Zionist project after the occupation of Palestine. Finally, an episode from Ismat’s Chughtai’s autobiography Kaaghazi hai Pairahan (1988), which narrates her own trial for obscenity charges against the pre-partition short story Lihaaf, will be used to examine politics of gender and respectability and the juridification of aesthetic discourses, particularly in the context of nationalism.We will approach our course texts as critical resources for thinking about the following themes:-- a appreciation of what can be learnt about the law through plurality of 'non-legal' genres that address it, including fiction, reportage and autobiography-- legality and the 'public sphere' under colonial regimes;--censorship and gender, and its role in the production of nationalist identities; -- the limitations and possibilities of legal processes in the face of extreme social and political violence;— genocide, war crimes, justice and moral responsibility, nationalism and historical trauma
303.Specific Scheduling Information: This is an elective course and will open to Second and Third Year Law students in Phase I, Phase II and the Add/Drop period.

3203.Title: Introduction to Legal Aspects of Merger and Acquisition law in Pakistan
3203.Description: This course introduces students to the legal architecture of M&A, Private Equity, and corporate combinations in Pakistan. It moves from foundational concepts and the regulatory landscape (SECP, CCP, the takeover code) through the lifecycle of a transaction, structuring, due diligence, negotiation, documentation, regulatory approvals, tax, and post-closing integration, and closes with cross-border transactions, ethical issues, and dispute resolution. The course emphasises the practical work of M&A lawyers: drafting, issue-spotting, and risk allocation.

3214.Title: Law and Regulations of Finance
3214.Description: At present, LUMS does not offer a single course that provides students with an understanding of the legal dimensions of finance. This course seeks to fill that gap by catering specifically to students of law, business, and economics, while also offering value to the wider university community.Law and Regulation of Finance (LRF) introduces students to the role of law in the functioning of financial institutions and markets, including banks, stock exchanges, insurance companies, fintech, and Islamic finance. It further engages students with pressing ethical and regulatory challenges, such as those contributing to credit crises, financial booms, and busts.In the context of Pakistan, the course explores how recurring IMF bailouts—typically negotiated every five years—shape the country’s economic and political landscape. By examining the legal underpinnings of Pakistan’s engagement with the IMF and other international financial institutions, students will gain a critical understanding of how global financial governance intersects with domestic law and policy.
3214.Specific Scheduling Information: Only Second Year Law (SYL) and Third Year Law (TYL) students in enrollment Phase II and Open to second and third-year law students, SDSB (ACF and MGS) seniors, and MGSHSS ECON, ECON/POL and ECON/MATH seniors in the Add/Drop period.As an advanced elective, prior coursework in contract law or company/corporate law is recommended.

3224.Title: Economic Development and Project Financing in Asia
3224.Description: This course examines the relationship between international economic development, capital flows, and the financing of large-scale infrastructure projects with an Asian centric focus. It explores how legal institutions, financial markets, governments, and multilateral organizations interact to facilitate economic growth through infrastructure investment. The first part of the course introduces students to the legal architecture of the international economic order, including the roles of international financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank Group, International Finance Corporation (IFC), and International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID). It also considers the prevailing legal and economic theories of economic development such as trade liberalization, capital mobility, and foreign direct investment.The second part evaluates such economic framework and theories from a real world perspective, comparing competing models of development in Asia, with particular emphasis on the experiences of the Asian Tigers, China, Pakistan, and the Gulf states. Students will critically assess industrial policy and foreign investment/infrastructure-led development.The third part focuses from a practical perspective on project finance and infrastructure transactions. Students will study the principal sources of finance and core concepts such as non-recourse lending and use of Special Purpose Vehicls. They will examine project bankability, risk allocation, and resultant project structuring. Students will also be introduced to key project agreements, including concession agreements, EPC contracts, offtake agreements, shareholder arrangements, and political risk mitigation.The final part addresses dispute resolution in international infrastructure projects, including international commercial arbitration and investor–state arbitration. Through case studies drawn from Asia and beyond, students will develop an integrated understanding of how infrastructure projects are conceived, financed, structured, and resolved when disputes arise.
3224.Specific Scheduling Information: The course will open to SYL and TYL Law students in Phase I, Phase II and the Add/Drop period.

326.Title: Intellectual Property Law
326.Description: This course has been designed to explore the normative underpinnings of intellectual property law from the standpoint of other disciplines such as finance, philosophy, economics etc. The topics have been selected with the aim to familiarize students with the important concepts of intellectual property law and to illustrate how these concepts explain the existing structure of copyright law, patent law and trademark law. Consequently, this course is not limited to the study of IP law of any one jurisdiction. At the end of this course, students should be able to critically engage with important concepts of intellectual property and understand the broad themes and debates that have shaped the law as it exists today.

352.Title: Public International Law
352.Description: This course is an introduction to Public International Law; it covers its sources, institutions and processes. Specific topics covered include human rights law, environmental protection, the law of sovereignty and self-defense. Recent challenges confronting international law will be studied and solutions and prescriptions will accordingly be posited. A wide and diverse range of contemporary international law issues including those relating to reproductive rights, the international financial order and the political and social freedoms of indigenous people will be investigated. As a whole, this course will engage with both theoretical and practical constructs of international law.
352.Specific Scheduling Information: This core course will open to Second Year Law students in enrollment Phase I and will open to Third Year and will remain open to Second Year Law students in Phase II and the Add/Drop period.

353.Title: Human Rights
353.Description: This course offers a wide-ranging exploration of international and comparative human rights law in context. It aims to equip students with sound grounding in history and philosophy of human rights as well as practical skills in human rights advocacy, litigation, and research. We will draw on jurisprudence of international and regional human rights bodies as well as domestic courts of Canada, India, Israel, Namibia, Pakistan, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The course is broadly divided into three parts. In the first part, we will explore the normative foundations, history, legal sources, adjudication techniques, and the institutional architecture of the global human rights regime. In the second part, we will turn to selected substantive rights such as the right to life, freedom from torture and ill-treatment, freedom of expression, and the right to health. Finally, in the last three seminars, we will take stock of some persistent challenges, such as securing the rights of children and women, and dealing with mass atrocities: genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity.
353.Specific Scheduling Information: The course will open to Second and Third Year Law students in enrollment Phase I, Phase II and the Add/Drop period.

4505.Title: Business and Human Rights: A Critical Legal Perspective from the South
4505.Description: This course is designed to deconstruct the paradigm of Business and Human Rights to see why it is alleged to be a discourse of market-friendly neoliberal philosophy, a tool to give legitimacy to corporations, and a continuity of the colonial nature of international law. To explore this, the course uses a critical legal theoretical lens from a Third World/South perspective in an interdisciplinary manner. Going back to the colonial roots of international law and mesmerizing nuances of neocolonialism, dependency theory, and deconstructive postcolonial theory, this course is extensive engagement with mainstream thinking of Business and Human Rights, intricacy of discussions of corporate governance, and an elaborate discussion with recent cases against corporations involving human rights violations.Despite embracing human rights rhetoric, this course wants to know how the concepts of ‘corporate personality,’ ‘limited liability,’ ‘lifting the corporate veil,’ and consequent ‘disclosure and transparency’ corporate decision-making around shareholder value theory vis-à-vis stakeholder theory and, above all, jurisprudential and jurisdictional issues around parent and subsidiary corporation in Global Value Chains, still serve the interests of the business. UN's approach to ‘Protect, Respect, and Remedy’ in its Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights expects weak states to Protect human rights. It requests powerful corporations to respect human rights and unrealistically seek remedies from theoretically and practically unequipped international legal mechanisms. This approach itself seems reflective of asymmetrical power relations of private political authority of corporations, that is, an integrated strategic reality of GVCs and International Financial Institutions vis-à-vis public responsibility of states. How can the weak states and the marginalized of these states hold corporations accountable? More than this, transcending moralist formal human rights, this course will try to recall substantive re-distributional aspects in the first call of the Third World to hold corporations accountable in the 1970s in New International Economic Order (NIEO) to contemporary social movements and ask how we can assure the redistribution of profits of corporations and global resources.
4505.Specific Scheduling Information: The course will open to Second and Third Year Law students in enrollment Phase I, Phase II and the Add/Drop period.

4812.Title: Legal Practice II: Legal Instruments
4812.Description: Legal Practice II is designed to prepare law students for the world of legal practice and is divided into three components: thinking; communication and drafting.While recognizing that entering the professional world will always carry its own learnings which are crucial for the development of a legal practitioner, this course seeks to equip its participants with the basic skills needed to excel. The idea that drives this course is to create a world as close to the reality of the life of a lawyer to best prepare the student for a potential career in law. 4925.Title: Women and the Criminal Law: The Pursuit for Justice
4925.Description: This course aims to offer students a critical understanding of women’s position within and treatment by the criminal law. It approaches this subject from a theoretical perspective, drawing on feminist legal theory and criminology scholarship to explore how the criminal law conceptualizes, is determined by and responds to gender. It locates this theoretical framework in women’s lived experiences with the criminal justice system– as victims, survivors and defendants – by drawing on relevant statutory provisions, case-law and empirical studies in instances of sexual violence, domestic violence, harassment, honour killing, child-marriage, and other harmful practices. This course primarily focuses on the Pakistani context, but also engages with broader comparative and international scholarship, more specifically from the South Asian region, to evaluate the pursuit of gender justice by and through the criminal law.

582.Title: Alternative Dispute Resolution
582.Description: Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) has become an increasingly important component of contemporary legal practice. As courts around the world confront rising caseloads, increasing costs, and delays in adjudication, parties are increasingly turning to alternative mechanisms for the resolution of disputes. ADR encompasses a range of processes, including negotiation, mediation, and arbitration, each of which offers distinct advantages and limitations depending upon the nature of the dispute and the interests of the parties involved.This course introduces students to the theory, law, and practice of ADR, with particular emphasis on the Pakistani legal framework and contemporary international developments. Students will examine the historical, cultural, and legal foundations of dispute resolution, before exploring the modern evolution of negotiation, mediation, and arbitration as professional dispute-resolution processes.The course combines doctrinal study with practical skills training. Students will develop negotiation, mediation, and arbitration advocacy skills through simulations, workshops, and problem-based exercises. By integrating theory, doctrine, and practical application, the course aims to equip students with the knowledge and skills required to advise clients on dispute-resolution strategy, participate effectively in ADR proceedings, and critically evaluate the role of ADR within contemporary justice systems.
582.Specific Scheduling Information: This is an elective course for LLM students and will remain closed for self-service enrollment during Enrollment Phases I and II.

204.Title: Introduction to Formal Mathematics
204.Description: Mathematics is created by the interplay between formal and informal, proof by logic and discovery by intuition. In this course, the student will see this interplay, learn simple proof techniques and heuristics, and come to appreciate the notion of mathematical structure

210.Title: Introduction to Differential Equations
210.Description: The laws of science and engineering are typically expressed in differential equations, which are equations with derivatives in them. Understanding of differential equations and their solutions is important in the sciences and engineering. This course deals with: First order differential equations; modeling; second order linear equations; Damped motion in mechanical and electrical systems; System of first order linear equations; Eigenvalues and Eigen vector; Series solutions; Introduction to special functions; Fourier series; Partial differential equations; separation of variables and Sturm-Liouville problems

222.Title: Linear Algebra II
222.Description: A brief review of the course LA-1 and Linear algebra with differential equations, Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors, Inner-Product Spaces, Operators on Inner-Product Spaces, Dual Vector Spaces, Quotient spaces, Direct Sums, Applications, Infinite dimensional linear spaces.

232.Title: Introduction to Game Theory
232.Description: Game Theory is the study of strategic situations i.e. where the outcomes for individuals depends on their own actions as well as the actions of others. As such it has a wide range of applications in many fields including Economics, Political Science, Law and Sports. This course introduces the fundamental principles, techniques and notation of Game Theory as well as some basic insights provided by some well-known games

252.Title: Discrete Mathematics
252.Description: This course covers the mathematical foundations of computer science. The aim is to introduce the students to the fundamental techniques of discrete mathematics, which may be employed in a variety of mathematical disciplines, including fields in theoretical computer science, such as, algorithms, data structures and complexity theory. An introduction to logic, proof techniques, sets, functions, and relations is made, along with an initiation to combinatorics, basic graph and tree structures. A very brief introduction to number theory and discrete probability is made. Problems are formed mathematically and solved using available tools and techniques

309.Title: Introduction to Analysis II
309.Description: Introduction to Analysis II is the sequel to Introduction to Analysis I, and together these two courses constitute the foundations of real analysis in mathematics. This course is designed to prepare students for future advanced analysis and functional analysis courses. It lays the foundation for several other areas, such as complex analysis, topology, dynamical systems, quantum mechanics, and mathematical statistics. The rigorous treatment of the subject in terms of theory and examples gives students the flavor of mathematical reasoning and intuition for other advanced topics in mathematics. Topics covered are Open, closed, and compact sets of real numbers. Sequences and series of functions, point wise and uniform convergence. Power series and Taylor series. Metric spaces: basic notions generalized from the setting of the real numbers

341.Title: Operations Research I
341.Description: Operations research has had an increasingly great impact on the management of organizations, including business, government, and military. Operations research involves formulation of real life situations into mathematical models, and then developing optimal solutions by application of various algorithms. The purpose of this course is to provide an appreciation of various techniques used in operations research, and their application in developing optimal solutions for real life problems.

407.Title: General Topology
407.Description: This course has been designed as an introduction to general topology. The student enrolled in this course should have a back-ground in Set Theory (and preferably some knowledge of Real Analysis - I). This course covers basic point set topology, in particular, Metric and Topological spaces, Separation Axioms, Connectedness, Compactness, Product spaces and Quotient topology. We will, also cover some algebraic topology, i.e. fundamental groups of topological spaces.

412.Title: Partial Differential Equations
412.Description: Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) permeate various scientific disciplines. This course deals with: Terminology; boundary and initial value problems; well- and ill-posed problems. the Laplace, wave and diffusion equations; the Klein-Gordon equation; Method of characteristics, separation of variables, integral transforms, Green's functions; potential scattering; dispersion and diffusion; regular and singular perturbation theory; asymptotics for complete solutions; Nonlinear PDEs: Converting nonlinear equations into linear PDEs; some exactly solvable cases; dimensional analysis and similarity; traveling waves; nonlinear diffusion and dispersion; the KdV, nonlinear Schrödinger and Sine-Gordon equations; reaction-diffusion equations; Fisher's equation; singular perturbations: boundary layers, homogenization. Variational Methods. Free-boundary value problems.

437.Description: Summer 2021 Course Description:-----------------------------------------------This is a first course in Stochastic Processes. The applications will be drawn from Finance, Physics, Biology and Medicine.A key component of the course will be the homework, where both theoretical and computational problems will be assigned. 439.Title: Applied Probability
439.Description: This is an intermediate level course focusing on the application of probability theory to science and engineering disciplines.The first portion of the course reviews the basic probability theory with some examples chosen from science and engineering. Laterportion of the course deals with moderately advanced topics that signify the use of probability theory in these disciplines.The topics covered in the course should help the students building a background for understanding and conducting research incomputer and data sciences, estimation and learning, and other more general engineering problems. In particular, we will discussrandom variables and expectations, joint and conditional distributions, random processes, queueing systems and Markov chains,confidence intervals, and prediction/learning/estimation theory.One important application area we will cover in the course is queueing theory.Why queuing theory? Any system (e.g., a web server, a customer service center) that has finite capacity and provides a servicecan potentially be modeled using queuing theory, which provides us with tools to predict system performance as well as designsystems that achieve high performance. For example, using queuing theory we can answer questions such as “What is the averagedelay experienced by requests arriving at a web server?” and “Given demand and a size of a given hospital, how many doctorsshould be hired to ensure that the no patient waits for longer than 10mins with high, say 98 percent, probability?”).We will also provide a brief introduction to machine learning, another important application area that has gained recent popularity.Why machine learning? Computers are increasingly being used as data analysis tools to obtain insights from the enormous amountsof data that is being collected in a variety of fields (now referred to as “big data”). Probability theory is now used as one of thekey methods for designing new algorithms to model such data, allowing, for example, a computer to make predictions aboutuncertain or new events. A use case would be to predict the weather tomorrow given weather data for past 10 years.A key goal of this course is to act as a bridge between the theoretical foundations of probability and its applications.

4418.Title: Numerical Linear Algebra
4418.Description: Linear Algebra is one of the most widely used topics in the mathematical sciences. In the course of Linear Algebra we learnt standard techniques for basic linear algebra tasks including the solution of linear systems, finding eigenvalues/eigenvectors and orthogonalisation of bases. However, these techniques are usually computationally too intensive to be used for the large matrices encountered in practical applications.This course will focus on the fundamental concepts of numerical linear algebra introducing the practical issues to practical applications. It will teach you how to analyze and apply certain algorithms in a reliable and computationally efficient way.We will focus on the following: direct and iterative methods for solving simultaneous linear equations; matrix factorization, decomposition, and transformation; conditioning, stability and efficiency; computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Since many real world problems ultimately reduce to linear algebra conceptsand algorithms, there will be a strong emphasis on understanding the advantages and disadvantages, and the limits of applicability for all the covered techniques.The course includes significant computing-related assignments will require the use of a computer and basic programming skills (Python). The theoretical material will be assessed in an examination over LMS/Zoom.

The theoretical material will be assessed in an examination over LMS/Zoom.

547.Title: Operational Research I
547.Description: Operations research has had an increasingly great impact on the management of organizations, including business, government, and military. Operations research involves formulation of real life situations into mathematical models, and then developing optimal solutions by application of various algorithms. The purpose of this course is to provide an appreciation of various techniques used in operations research, and their application in developing optimal solutions for real life problems.

111.Title: Principles of Microeconomics
111.Description: This course teaches basic microeconomic concepts and their implications for individuals and firms. Attention will be paid to understanding the decision-making process of households, business firms and government, and consequent allocation of resource and price determination under different market structures. Market equilibrium conditions will be discussed in the short run and the long run under various market models. This course is meant to foster critical evaluation of standard economic concepts such as scarcity and choice, demand and supply, cost and productions, government intervention & market failure, price mechanism, the efficient allocation of scarce resources and concludes with game theory

2201.Title: Introduction to Business Economics
2201.Description: IntroductionEconomics drives business, enables policy formulation and impacts people in their daily lives. This course stresses the economic investigation of crucial business functions. It provides a basic overview of the principles of economics and explain how to apply these principles to support decision making in businesses. This is an introductory course for students from different backgrounds to gain a basic understanding of Economics for Business, to enable them to study advanced courses at the master’s level. With the division of the course into Microeconomics and Macroeconomics components: The Microeconomics for Business section examines how consumers and firms make decisions and how they interact with each other in markets. Topics covered include theory and applications of supply and demand, consumer and firm behavior and price determination. The Macroeconomics for Business section studies the basic concepts such as National Income Accounts, Gross Domestic Product, Unemployment and the basics of the Open Economy. Aims The aim of this short course is to introduce students to the core economic principles and how these can be used in a business environment to help decision making and behavior. It provides the fundamental concepts of microeconomics that explain how economic agents make decisions and how these decisions interact. It explores the principles underlying macroeconomics that explain how the economic system works, where it fails and how decisions taken by economic agents affect the economic system.

5201.Title: Business Economics
5201.Description: This course is designed for students studying economics in their graduate degrees in the field of management in which economic principles will be taught as they apply to the business environment. This course is split into two parts. Part one will focus on the application of microeconomic principles to individual and business decision-making. The topics falling under part 1 include business and economics, business and markets, background to demand and supply, decision making by firms, alternative business strategies, and relationship between government and business. Part two will focus on macroeconomic framework and environment in which firms operate. Beginning with the principal macroeconomic variables, we will discuss the role of money in the economy and explore the relationship between money, exchange rate and inflation. We will then construct an aggregate demand and aggregate supply model of price and output determination. Using this framework, we will study the role of monetary, fiscal and exchange rate policies in macroeconomic stabilization. We will also examine the mechanics of government intervention at the macro level as well as its impact on business and its potential benefits and drawbacks.

In tandem, the course will explore how issues such as organization structure, technology, innovation, ethics, corporate responsibility, competitive environment and customer-focus influence managerial decision making

242.Title: Business Ethics and Corporate Social Responsibility
242.Description: This course provides an introduction to ethics and their application in the arena of business. It begins with an exploration of theoretical concepts and related contestations in the area of moral philosophy. Thereafter, descriptions and analyses of the problems and challenges posed by ethical dilemmas in real-world situations, using the lens of the conceptual frameworks, form a major part of this course. To this end, issues on the levels of the individual, the organization and the system/society will be taken up as they relate to the internal and external stakeholders of businesses; furthermore, debates around the idea of corporate social responsibility and its use as a policy will be one of our focuses. Since the underpinnings of moral philosophy explored at the beginning of the course are primarily areligious, and since a broad perspective on ethics and morality should include the role of religion and culture, this becomes our point of departure for discussing the Islamic ethical philosophy and prescriptions for business

244.Title: Reforming The Public Sector
244.Description: The Course is designed for students who have preferably been exposed to various key areas of public management policy framework. After looking at some of the foundational aspects of the policy framework and implementation regime, it underlines the need for reforms to meet the multiple challenges of service delivery on a sustainable basis. It aims at identifying some critical connects between the public and the private sector with a view to meet the overall objective of growth and development. It tends to develop students interest and keenness in the public-sector management with a view to opt it as a career while broadening their profile.OverviewThe course aims at providing exposure and an understanding to the students about the working of public sector institutions as key drivers of growth, development and delivery system. It underlines the need and role of some critical dynamics and a process of reforms enabling the institutions to bring more efficiency and transparency in the delivery of public services. 247.Description: This course aims to provide students with an understanding of the principles and practices of public financial management (PFM) in Pakistan. 252.Title: Logic and Critical Thinking
252.Description: Even though thinking is a natural activity, much of our thinking is confounded by distortions, biases and prejudices, and is in many instances uninformed and partial. It would not be an exaggeration to say that the quality of our life depends in crucial ways on the quality of our thinking. Excellence in thought, however, requires systematic cultivation. This course introduces the tools and techniques of logic and critical thinking, and their systematic application in various arenas of life. Finally, through the application of a strategy for understanding, analyzing, and evaluating arguments, it will bring to life the process of thinking and the art of argumentation.

263.Title: Contemporary Social Policy Issues in Pakistan
263.Description: This course introduces undergraduate students to key social policy issues in Pakistan. It satisfies the information and analysis needs of future managers and practitioners in the fields of public policy, public management and development. It covers a wide range of topics, including poverty, social exclusion, social safety nets, education, food security, demography and housing. Students use recent data to critically analyze policy goals, delivery mechanisms and available policy choices on each of these topics. Further Details: This course responds to a market demand for graduates who can effectively apply their understanding of social issues to policy making and management in public and nonprofit sectors. Such growing demand has its roots in four recent developments. First, governments at federal, provincial and local levels have warmed up to the idea of attracting talent from the private sector to improve delivery of social services, instead of relying exclusively on the traditional civil service. Thus, we see various governments advertising positions at entry and middle/senior management levels in state-owned-corporations, autonomous organizations, publicly funded nonprofits and attached departments. Second, the number of government organizations working under a corporate governance structure has increased substantially over the past two decades (e.g. National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA), Earthquake Relief and Rehabilitation Authority). Third, the private sector now plays an increasingly large role in provision of several social services, including education and health, leading to the emergence of large school-chains and hospitals. Fourth, local and foreign NGOs and international aid agencies now play an important role in policy formulation and in delivery of social services. The combined effect of these developments is to create employment opportunities for professional managers in the social sector. These are attractive career positions for LUMS graduates.This course will help LUMS students in pursuing a future career in public and nonprofit sectors. By introducing students to contemporary issues and challenges in social policy, it will expose them to the working of the government, local and foreign NGOs, international aid agencies and private providers of social services. All of them are prospective employers. A broad overview of their governance structures, mandate, operational strategies and challenges will help students in job interviews. The course will act as a foundation course for students who intend to continue education in the fields of public management and public policy.Topics included in the course have been carefully selected based on their relevance for future career pursuits of LUMS students. These correspond to: 1) areas in which a government organization has recently advertised entry level or mid-career positions; or 2) important program activities of the nonprofit sector and private providers of social services. Examples of the former are: Prime Minister’s Program Delivery Unit; Power Generation and Distribution Companies; NADRA; District Education and Health Authorities. Examples of the latter are: large school chains; various projects of the USAID, CIDA, the World Bank and other donors.As a survey course, there is a natural tension between breadth and depth – between the number of topics addressed and the amount of attention given to each topic. In this course, the emphasis is on breadth and the overarching goal is to convey to students the policy dilemmas that public managers face in Pakistan.The course will comprise a series of 75-minute interactive lectures on topics identified below. These lectures will provide students an opportunity to critically analyze policy and implementation challenges in areas important for their professional careers. Students will be expected to read prescribed texts before coming to the class. On average, this will comprise 20-25 pages of reading per session. During the class, they will be provided a structured overview of the issue/challenge. The structured overview (usually a presentation by the instructor) will be grounded in theory but will present a practitioner’s perspective in each case. Specific examples from real life will be used to illustrate the policy challenge under discussion. Students will be expected to critically analyze policy questions during class discussions

348.Title: Internet Governance and Technology Policy
348.Description: We live in the Information Age and unlike the agricultural and industrial societies which took decades to evolve, the information age came upon us with a speed no one would have predicted. And it evolves every single day at a pace which is difficult to keep up with. Internet and Information Communication Technologies has a lot to do with this. It is only natural then that internet and related mediums become an integral part of our lives and generates all sorts of conversation on how it must be accessed, managed, regulated and used to benefit the society and general populace at large. The course outlines the key areas that students would require to understand internet –its architecture, layers, and the different global institutions that shape the internet as we see it. More important issues to that people are now openly talking about is freedom of speech in the context of online media, right to privacy, big data and how it includes and excludes, the age of algorithms, the debates on net neutrality amongst a few. Also critical is the understanding of the digital divide, on the lines of the socio-economic offline divides, and how technology can be used to empower and support groups, communities, businesses and society at large. The role of policy makers in providing Universal Access and enabling environment for tech businesses will also be understood.

Since this course attempts to cover several key challenges, it does not aim to explore any of these in great depth. 386.Description: This course explores the contested nexus of business, government and society. It examines different perspectives about the purpose of business, of the state and governance. It analyzes the socio-political environment that faces business and its influence on organizations, policymaking and society. A key theme of this course is labor relations, for this is the very center of business, government and society.The course explores how businesses exert their influence on the state to secure economic and political resources and how this affects its stakeholders, particularly workers, consumers and citizens. We will also review how neoliberal globalization has led to a rapidly changing dynamic between public policy and corporate power and how business has become a global driver in public policy. This will include discussions on private governance, corporate social responsibility, the role of NGOs, the influence of business in times of crises, and the emergence of the neoliberal state. The course ends on hope offered by the degrowth movement in the age of the Anthropocene.

387.Title: Managing Diverse People and Organizations
387.Description: This is an advanced course for students who want to develop a deeper understanding of diversity, equality and inclusion in management. The objective of the course is to develop a theoretically informed understanding of historical rationales behind diversity, current status of knowledge and practice of diversity in organizational and management context. The focus is to provide a practical understanding of how diversity actually works, while building a theoretical toolkit to enable students to become practitioners and influencers in the field of diversity management. Course material is therefore focused on participatory learning and practice (through case studies) and challenges specific to Pakistani context.This course is suitable for students who want to work in multicultural teams, who want to be leaders and entrepreneurs in an increasingly diverse business ecology by impacting how difference is managed in organizations and who want to change what we know about diversity as future researchers.This course is built on the philosophy that we learn from one another – consequently, there will be a strong emphasis on actively engaging in self-reflection, discussing assigned readings and real-world scenarios, sharing experiences, and participating in experiential learning exercises

389.Title: Fashion Management
389.Description: Fashion is everywhere! Infecting one and all, as Pakistani brands take the growing consumer market by storm. With the forever rising demand, there is indeed no shortage of supply. Back in the day, the unstructured clothing industry was powered by home based businesses, only till the time, the term ‘Fashion Industry’ was coined. It is then that the larger giants began to jump on to the band wagon and took the consumers by storm.This course aims at unraveling the mysteries of the Fashion Industry- from concept to consumer. Briefly touching on the structure of the industry, the course will move on to the various theories and myths that hold this industry in place. Every aspect of the business of fashion will be touched upon to elaborate the wider scope of fashion business management.The course aims to attract students who have in interest in this industry or have an existing business running. Whether it is a start-up idea they are toying with, a small business they are currently struggling with or aspire to take off their career in this industry in the future.Equipped with a course of this kind they will be able to better understand how to position their brand and product to their desired customer, using the correct marketing mediums along with strengthening the back of their brand by properly structuring the supply chain of such a business. Design philosophy and product strategy will be needed to fill in the gaps of the market. As the business becomes more competitive costing and pricing strategies come actively into play, which will all be incorporated in the course. Additionally, the course aims to create industry academia linkages with deep interaction and engagement with industry specialists

481.Title: Entrepreneurship
481.Description: Entrepreneurship is about turning an idea into a valuable enterprise under a certain level of uncertainty by remaining in control of what you want to achieve and how you want to achieve it”Welcome to be a part of the entrepreneurial revolution that has literally ‘infected’ the contemporary global thinking! No other jargon has so much in use in recent times as entrepreneurship, and it is certainly for a reason. That is, perhaps no other thing can be so powerful, sustainable and thrilling as the phenomenon of ‘new venture creation’ for its ability to solve the prevailing problem of the mankind in its entirety. It is an introductory course on entrepreneurship intended to enhance your ‘willingness’ to set out on an entrepreneurial journey and give you a chance to think about alternative career options available to you in an economy so full of unmet needs and so short of innovative solutions. In this semester we will assess, explore, critique and celebrate the phenomenon of entrepreneurship. This course will approach entrepreneurship as a mindset, an attitude and a behaviour to undertake value-creating initiatives in situations with a certain level of uncertainty that is expected to lead to the creation of a new business entity, be it a new start-up or a launch of new product or service within a large corporation. The course is designed in six modules with almost equal focus on the students’ development of both hard and soft entrepreneurial skills. The discussion in the first three modules will predominantly revolve around the cognitive part of the entrepreneurship process, which will allow the students to understand and challenge the very ‘logic’ of how expert entrepreneurs usually make decisions as opposed to a stereotypical manager working under a very different scheme of things. The last three modules of the course will then deal with some contemporary analytical tools used in the entrepreneurship education, coupled with certain ‘tricks of the trade’, to generally improve the students’ skills to develop a more innovative and sustainable business model for whatever entrepreneurial pursuit they ever plan to undertake. This course, therefore, promises a unique form of logic, which might at times be antagonistic to the conventional principles of management, but then it is what entrepreneurship is all about. Given the nature of the subject, the curriculum of this course will also ensure a substantial exposure to the living practice of entrepreneurship through certain assignments, case study discussions and the guest speaker sessions that will be organized in the university. Students will get an adequate chance to interact with different practicing entrepreneurs at different points along the course to validate their classroom learning and refine their business ideas. In short, this course promises a blend of fun and learning.

201.Title: Principles of Marketing
201.Description: Marketing helps in understanding the consumption requirements of our markets. It is through the process of marketing that firms deliver their products to consumers such that it creates a win-win situation both for the firm and for consumers. This course introduces, to the students, fundamental concepts related to the dynamics of consumption marketplace (e.g. market types, competitive landscape) and marketing tools (e.g. Segmentation/Targeting, Positioning, Product, Price, Promotion, Place) to successfully fulfill consumer needs and wants. The ultimate objective of all firm-customer interaction is to create and manage long term profitable customer relationships by creating more and more value for customers. This course will enhance students’ problem solving and decision making abilities towards marketing related issues using customer-centric approach

302.Title: Digital Marketing
302.Description: "Traditional media and its once unmatched power has been progressively eroded through the emergence of new communication technologies which make creating and distributing information an easy and low-cost exercise. This has caused a change in the balance of power, as even individuals are able to find global audiences with simple tools like blog entries and social media posts as well as other methods. This development has immediately and significantly affected marketing and public relations as age old strategies, standards and methodologies that relied on the power and reach of traditional media stand challenged. This course will examine real world cases, research and theory on a topic that has attracted much attention across the world in the past decade, i.e. the role of new media technologies in the fields of marketing and public relations. The course focuses particularly on the innovative use of media and communication tools, including but not limited to, social media networks, desktop publishing, web 2.0, satellite and cable television and interactive technologies. Students are encouraged to envision the innovative deployment of new media technologies in the fields of marketing, public relations guided by theoretical frameworks. Students will find this to be a hands-on course that will see them participate using most of the technologies mentioned. Participants in the course will be required to write online blogs, create low cost video and audio advertising and public relations responses, develop short research reports based on social media monitoring, and engage in a strategic war game that pits a mock organization versus individuals, using the full spectrum of media tools.Prior knowledge of the technologies mentioned is not a pre-requisite to the course as students will be fully oriented to the use of each tool as we progress in the course.NOTE: This course will require the students to own and bring to class one of the following: a smart phone, a tablet or a laptop computer. The students will get hands on experience with marketing and promotions using new media technologies, software and hardware innovations in interactive technology, social media communication, media channels and other avenues"Teaching Methodology:------------------------------->Teaching Methodology: blend of both synchronous and asynchronous>Lecture details: 50% recorded and 50% live interaction lectures tentativelyGRADING BREAKUP:------------------------------Field Digital Marketing Case Study: 20% (One week field research + One week writing and refinement)Discussion Posts: 20% (5 posts, each is two short paragraphs or audio and video responses– quizzes will only be administered if the instructor sees class need, otherwise the remaining 4% of this component will be applied to the discussion posts)Class Participation & Attendance*: 20%Midterm Examination: 20%Group Assignment (War Game): 20%Final Examination: None* Attendance both in-class and for online sessions is mandatory. There is no penalty for two unexcused absences, however every following unexcused absence will incur a 3% grade reduction from the CP and Attendance column (up to 18%). More than 6 unexcused absences will result in an automatic F. No excuse for an absence will be entertained more than 10 days after the absence. There are no makeup exams allowed, in the case of excused absences, the class average will be assigned.

332.Description: Marketing attempts to influence the way consumers behave. These attempts have implications for the organizations making them, the consumers they are trying to influence, and the society in which these attempts occur. We are all consumers and we are all members of society, so consumer behavior and its attempts to influence it, are critical to all of us. This course is designed to provide an understanding of consumer behavior. This understanding can make us better consumers, better marketers, and better citizens This Course consists of two blocks: Marketing Research and Consumer Behavior. First, learners will see the tools and methods to be able to effectively conduct (or hire) and interpret marketing research. Second, they will learn the foundations of consumer behavior and the consumer decision-making process and how to use this knowledge in the formulation of effective marketing strategies and tactic.

392.Title: Brand Management
392.Description: A brand is one of the firm’s most valuable assets. This course aims to outline the concept of brand equity and how its potential effects and tradeoffs impact the brand. The Brand Equity concept enables the brand to be distinguished from its unbranded commodity counterpart and is the sum total of consumers’ perceptions & feelings about the product’s attributes and how they perform, and about the brand name and what it stands for. This course will aim to illustrate how by creating perceived differences among products through branding and by developing a loyal consumer franchise, marketers create value that can translate to financial profits.Students in this course will review a comprehensive and updated treatment of the subjects of brand, brand equity and brand management leading to the design and implementation of marketing programs and activities requisite to build, measure, and manage brand equity. Specifically, students will learn:•	The role of brands, concept of brand equity and advantages of creating strong brands•	3 ways to build brand equity via selection of brand elements, marketing programs and activities by leveraging secondary associations•	Different approaches to measuring brand equity and how to implement a brand equity measurement system•	Alternative branding strategies and how to devise brand hierarchies and portfolios•	The role of corporate brands, family brands, individual-brands, modifiers and how to combine them into sub-brands.•	How to adjust branding strategies over time and across geographic boundaries to maximize brand equity•	How to conduct a Brand AuditThis course will be taught from a marketing practitioner’s point of view with the aim to enrich the course student’s understanding of the local marketing context and its connect with global best practices

5401.Description: As a core course this aims to develop a solid understanding of the basic terminologies, concepts, tools, and frameworks in marketing management. A broad range of marketing decisions in a variety of consumer settings will be covered through a marketing simulation. The gamification concept engages the students with a diversified background into an immersive experiential learning environment.The course will also address recent shifts and trends resulting in digital tool kit. This shifting environment presents new opportunities and challenges for marketers.Among the topics discussed in the course are consumer and industrial buying behavior, market segmentation, product positioning, elements of the marketing mix (such as, product development, pricing strategy, integrated marketing communications, and channel strategies), break-even analysis, CRM and marketing research techniques. 5301.Title: Organizations and Leadership
5301.Description: Overview: Leadership effectiveness is central to organizational success. Leaders exercise a critical role in defining the purpose, strategy, and direction of an organization. They set in place the structures, processes, and systems through which organizations achieve their goals. Through role modeling, leaders set the culture that determines how organizations actually operate and how people go about doing their work on regular basis. Finally, leaders steer organizations through turbulences and upheavals toward sustainability and growth by managing and leading the change process. This course has been designed to prepare the students in assuming their responsibilities as leaders working in for-profit and nonprofit organizations in the private, public, and social sectors of Pakistan.Description: This course seeks to provide students with a fundamental grasp of the interactions that occur among people in the workplace and in institutional contexts. It will afford tools to understand and evaluate individual, group, and organizational processes. The student will gain an appreciation of the relevance of the study of organizational behavior in relation to the application and responses to public policies and regulations influencing their processes. The course will further encourage students to think about and develop personal skills that are central to leadership. 320.Title: Comparative Politics
320.Description: This module focused on Comparative Politics (CP) as a subfield of political science. 2214.Title: Decolonizing Democracy: Lessons from the Global South
2214.Description: Popular Western discourses and academic political science literature take democracy as the end-goal to which all non-Western countries must aspire. But what, exactly, is democracy? If it means “rule of the people,” then is democracy compatible with inequalities of wealth and power? Can countries claim democracy if their national sovereignty is compromised—or if they compromise the national sovereignty of others? Is democracy a Western concept foreign to the Global South to begin with?Academic political science literature takes as its default the liberal-democratic model, which originated in Europe and North America to promote capitalist-market society alongside colonial-imperialist expansion. In contrast, working-class and anti-colonial movements have often sought to achieve democracy not only by freeing themselves from liberal democracies, but by transcending the liberal-democratic model’s theoretical and institutional boundaries. What alternative forms of democracy have they conceptualized and practiced?This course thus operates at the intersection of political theory and comparative politics by bringing the political science literature on democracy into conversation with recent engagements with decolonization. The first part of the course draws on political theory to enquire into the sufficiency of minimalistic or “thin” definitions of democracy in most comparative politics literature. The second part turns critical attention towards recent discussions of decolonization and imperialism, particularly debates between epistemological-cultural approaches and material-political approaches, and how they may guide conceptualization of democracy. The third part of the course examines a range of self-proclaimed democratic projects in Latin America, Africa, and Asia, and asks whether we should take their claims to popular legitimacy seriously, and whether they may have lessons to offer to arrive at a “decolonized” understanding of democracy.

268.Title: Master Narratives: Minding Gender and Media Gaps
268.Description: The following course aims to utilize various critical tools established to identify, contextualize, and counter grand narratives initially set forth by Lyotard in his seminal work ‘The Postmodern Condition: A Report on Knowledge’. The course will demonstrate how these narratives interplay with various subjects discussed in global, regional, and local media and will additionally examine how gender plays a crucial role in comprehending and deconstructing these narratives. Students will unpack ideological, social, and structural themes such as language, culture, gender, nationalism, governance, race, conflict, human rights, and religion as Metanarratives through the lens of print and electronic media coverage on these subjects. The primary lens the course will utilize to explore these themes will involve analyzing how the Media is helping frame existing narratives and how it can be used to counter those very narratives. Additionally, each major master-narrative will be examined through the lens of how gender is incorporated into the metanarrative. An additional regional filter of South Asia and more specifically Pakistan, will be added to all the subjects discussed in class and students will distil the literature and media output in a localized context for policy analysis.The proposed course aims to help students understand the subtleties of critical thinking and produce original work based on how the themes brought up in class interplay in a global and local information landscape. One of the frameworks used for this purpose is the theory of ‘Glocalization’, introduced by Sociologist Roland Robertson in 1997 referring to ‘the simultaneity - the co-presence - of both universalizing and particularizing tendencies’. Media analysis will allow students to observe and trace how media coverage on these issues is being disseminated from global to local levels and how this coverage and framing is implicitly or explicitly gendered in nature.Each session will explore a new topic and apply these broader analysis tools to the chosen subject i.e. The China Pakistan Economic Corridor, Cultural Appropriation, Election campaign trail, Israel’s bombardment of Gaza etc. Some topic sessions (3) will be left open to revision to make room for subjects under media scrutiny at the time of teaching. Given the subjective and interdisciplinary nature of media debate on contemporary issues, there are always various intersecting themes under discussion. For this reason, the individual sessions will be slotted into three broad zones to allow for a comprehensive unpacking of theoretical frameworks informing each zone. These include an analysis of how the media deals differently with values and philosophies under ‘Ideology’ i.e. Nationalism, Democracy etc, as opposed to institutional ‘Structure’ i.e. Governments and Courts. The final domain ‘Society’, will explore subjects that encompass media coverage on interpersonal themes such as Gender, Race, Religion etc.All the individual sessions will be clumped together under three broad themes, the use of- Ideology- Structure- Society*Although to some degree all these broad zones are in and of themselves intersectional frames and many of the topics can be slotted under all three zones simultaneously, for the purposes of this course the use of ‘Ideology’, ‘Structure’ and ‘Society’ are indicative of epistemological framing and subsequent constraints in how media analysis for each section will be framed. The sessions allocated under Ideology will deal primarily with theoretical underpinnings and conflicting definitions in metanarratives of Nationhood, Religion etc. In the case of themes slotted under Structure the focus will be on a methodological unpacking of how hierarchies and systems operate and are organized. Students will examine metanarratives for where power is located in each structure. Finally, sessions in the Society section will negotiate metanarratives of contemporary ‘Culture Wars’ and students will write from a position that incorporates lived experience. Each of these broad categories allow students to apply a variety of selective methodological approaches to each of their three papers and to unpack media and gender metanarratives from these chosen stand points.Students shall explore these subjects in class sessions through in-class written assignments and by framing counter narratives for each subject. There will be three core Master narrative essays, where students will write a 1300-1500 word research paper identifying a media and gendered Meta-narrative, exploring it’s dissemination at the global and local level and contextualizing its various applications in a Pakistani context.Another key element of the course includes a group project that will involve students developing a Pakistani Media counter-narrative on any of the broad themes mentioned. The format for this will project will include a short documentary.Each topic will be explored in class through key texts, classical and contemporary debate on the subject demonstrated through visual aids.

A young Nietzsche would claim that there is a poet (Shakespeare/Hamlet) who teaches us to glimpse into the cruel ‘truth’ of being and in so doing tries to save us as a healing magician, perhaps. This course then, is an attempt to think slowly with Shakespeare the praxes of polis i.e. political philosophy under the spell of poetry’s magic.

335.Title: Revolutionary War and Counterinsurgency
335.Description: The purpose of this course is to explore one of the most common forms of conflict of the 20th and early 21st centuries, which can be loosely categorized under the term ‘irregular warfare.’ This form of conflict was characteristic of the guerrilla struggles waged by many anti-colonial liberation movements against their colonial occupiers, from the 1940s to the 1970s. It was employed by communist revolutionaries against established governments in China and South Vietnam. Since then, it has come to be used by a variety of very different movements – for example, the Palestinian Liberation Organization, the Afghan Taliban, the Sri Lankan Tamil Tigers – in situations ranging from civil wars to separatist struggles to latter day terrorism. Ultimately, the common feature uniting the conflicts discussed in this course is that they are asymmetric, with the government enjoying clear military superiority over the insurgents. Consequently, the focus of conflict becomes the political, rather than the military, with popular support considered to be the key to claiming victory. The course begins by introducing students to important concepts in the study of revolutionary war and counterinsurgency, focusing on the political dimension of such conflicts. The course then embarks on a global survey of insurgencies of the 20th and early 21st century, ranging from Asia and Africa to Latin America. In each week, a different aspect of insurgency is discussed (for example, class struggle, fragmentation, violence towards civilians), and one or more movements that highlight varying dimensions of that aspect are examined. Towards the end of the course, irregular conflicts relating to Pakistan are discussed and students are encouraged to apply their understanding of the concepts discussed in class to these conflicts.Course Objectives:1.	Introduce students to theoretical concepts underpinning revolutionary conflicts and insurgencies, demonstrating their distinctness from conventional warfare and the paramount importance of political considerations in such conflicts.2.	Familiarize students with the history and political dynamics of a number of important conflicts ranging from the mid-20th to the early 21st century and spanning more than three continents.3.	Encourage students to develop their writing and analytical skills and apply the concepts taught in the course through in-depth essays on a) a chosen international conflict, and b) a chosen conflict related to Pakistan.

379.Title: US Imperialism
379.Description: With more than 900 bases around the world, the United States maintains a global presence that outstretches any empire in history despite ostensibly being just a nation-state. Concentrated around global trade chokepoints and key sites of production and extraction, this constellation of military outposts lays the foundation for an ""imperialism of free trade"": a system in which military dominance guarantees ready access for capital to all corners of the world and the power to set the terms of participation in global markets. This course develops a precise understanding of that system, its historical origins, and the particular character of its latest and most consequential iteration under US power.We begin with the hypothesis that while there have been innumerable empires in our past, imperialism is something far rarer. Only two other powers have attempted it, the Portuguese with their enforced commercial licenses, and the British as self-appointed guardians of the free seas. Building on this legacy and taking lessons from their failures, the United States realized a distinctly anti-colonial form of imperialism, operating through de jure sovereign nation-states instead of foreign dominions. This configuration, anchored by a global network of military bases and the infrastructure of dollar supremacy, promised invisibility and with it longevity. The possibility of being everywhere without being anywhere. Lifting the cloak it claims for itself, through the course we track two inextricably related mechanisms that make its power visible: (1) coercive authority through a global military base network, arms sales, and covert operations, and (2) less overtly coercive power to shape markets and capital flows through dollar dominance, key commodity production control, international institutions, and sanction threats.Having developed a conceptual and historical map of US imperialism, in the last part of the course we reassess the short life of the Washington Consensus world. For a brief moment in the 1990s, with the fall of the Berlin Wall and China's entry into the WTO, the American order felt not just universal but permanent. That confidence did not survive the Global War on Terror, and it has not survived the rise of alternate centers of military and market power. One can already dream of obituaries. But the death of US primacy will not be the death of US imperialism. Just as colonial withdrawal only created a postcolonial world, structured by the very forces it claimed to leave behind, American retreat will leave us in a post-American order still built in its image. This course provides the empirical grounding and conceptual vocabulary to understand not only how that order was constructed but what it will leave behind.

464.Title: Political Sociology
464.Description: Political Sociology investigates the social bases of politics and the impact of politics on society. Since World War II, and the 1960s in particular, the steady growth of interest, literature, and debate on state-society relations has translated into the constitution of Political Sociology as a subfield of Sociology and/or Political Science (the classification varies according to countries). In France, Political Sociology is considered an integral part of Political Science (along with Political Theory, Public Policy, Comparative Politics and International Relations). In UK, the London School of Economics (LSE) offers an MSc in Political Sociology, based in the department of Sociology, leading to an ample range of professions (teaching, research, public administration, social services, journalism, publishing, think tanks, NGOs, among others).After a brief introduction to Political Sociology and a discussion of its core issue, i.e. the social foundations of power, the course explores the work of Marx and Weber and how it has informed subsequent debate within political sociology. The course then analyses a variety of different political phenomena and processes, including the state and its manifestations, social cleavages and the interests and identities they generate, the roots and forms of political action, and transnational phenomena.

263.Title: The Making of the Islamic world
263.Description: What did it mean to belong to the Islamic world, and who decided that? How was political authority established after the Prophet, and what made it legitimate? How did a loose community become an empire, and how was that empire governed across vast distances? What did everyday life look like in cities such as Baghdad, and how were these worlds connected through trade, travel, and networks of knowledge? And how do we know any of this—what kinds of sources do historians use, and how should they be read?This course explores these questions through the emergence of Islam and the formation of an Islamic imperium between the seventh and thirteenth centuries, with a focus on the Middle Eastern heartlands. Rather than tracing rulers and dynasties, it examines how political authority, social and economic life, and cultural production took shape across changing geographies. Drawing on primary sources, the course invites students to reconstruct this world and to think critically about how the “Islamic” is defined and studied.

6101.Title: Operations and Supply Chain Strategy
6101.Description: Operations transform resource or data inputs into desired goods, services, or results, to create value for customers and the manufacturer or service provider. Operations in automotive industry may involve production of engine or body parts or automotive assembly. In banking, operations may involve providing teller services to the customers. Similarly, at McDonalds operations may involve producing Big Mac or French fries. A primary objective of any manager (regardless of the industry type) is to design, plan and execute these operations in a cost-effective and timely manner. Operations management thereby encompass all the various business activities right from the product design phase through its manufacturing till the delivery of the final product to the end consumer. Supply chain management concepts are therefore seen an extension of the basic understanding of operations management. A thorough understanding of intricacies of operations and supply chain management functions is second to none in importance both for manufacturing as well as service-oriented firms.A strategic orientation towards operations management can help firm outperform its competitors in long run. A well-crafted operations and supply chain strategy (OSCS) remains instrumental in achieving sustainable competitive advantage in today’s business world. Accordingly, this course Intends to develop strategic understanding of operations and supply chain management of its participants. Emphasis will be to enable students appreciate the far-reaching consequences of operations and supply chain management related decisions in enhancing the profitability and growth of modern firms.

6401.Title: Applied Research and Analysis
6401.Description: This course is designed to develop data analytic skills of students to become sophisticated producers and consumers of empirically grounded practices in businesses and public policy. The course will help students to interpret evidence clearly and concisely to improve the speed, reliability, and quality of decisions. The concept learned in this class should help students identify opportunities in which data analytics can be used to improve performance and support important decisions. To gain a greater understanding and familiarity with the growing use of “Big Data” in decision making, students will work intensively with real world data, drawing from examples in business and public policy, to develop the skills to use data in making informed decisions.The students are expected to work on STATA to explore real world problems/questions, develop hypothesis and perform basic statistical analysis on the questions of interest they chose for empirical projects using real world data sets, such as Pakistan Demographic and Health Surveys (PDHS), Health Insurance Subsidy Program (HISP), Pakistan Labor Force Surveys (PLFS), and Pakistan Enterprise Surveys (PES). Data sets will be provided.

100.Title: Introduction to Sociology
100.Description: This is a survey course that aims to introduce students to the origins of the discipline of Sociology, and provide them with a sociological perspective on a range of socio-political issues. We will focus on three central themes- social change, social inequality, and social harmony versus conflict- and combine selective theoretical texts with case studies to study the mechanisms and institutions that can trigger, foster, sustain, or undermine each of the three processes. The theoretical texts introduce students to the origins, basic premises, and key concerns of the discipline. The case studies introduce students to a variety of conceptual tools and methodological approaches used in sociological research and analysis

223.Title: Sociology of Education
223.Description: The education system is both a source of perpetuating socio-economic inequalities, and a tool for challenging the status quo. Educational institutions, especially schools are an integral part of the socialization process, preparing the next generation to take on their role as “social” actors. The course examines how and why the education system perpetuates or challenges existing inequalities within society. It introduces students to sociological theories of education, examining the intersection between education, class, culture, gender, resistance and democracy. The first part provides a macro level analysis of education and its place within society by introducing students to grand theories of education with a particular emphasis on functionalism, pragmatism, and critical pedagogy. The second part focuses on the formalized education system, in particular the school, examining the structure and organization of the school, teaching and pedagogy, classroom inequalities, and the politics of language and curriculum. The third part explores contemporary debates on technology and AI and its role in the formal education system. The readings therefore move from a macro level analysis to the micro unit of the school, highlighting both the potential and the limitation of modern day schooling in challenging existing inequalities within society.

226.Title: Disasters and Society
226.Description: Current trends of increasing urbanization, the reality of climate change, threats of industrial and biological hazards, have made disasters commonplace. But there is nothing ordinary about disasters. Disasters are stress-inducing, complex events that are difficult to manage and recover from. This course introduces students to the field of disaster studies and disaster theory utilizing an interdisciplinary and a multi-disciplinary approach. The first part of the course discusses what disasters are and why they need to be studied. It provides an overview and comparison between ancient and modern disasters emphasizing the intersection between the human system and the environment. During this course disasters are discussed and framed both as highly complex events to manage, and as opportunities to learn lessons and mitigate future catastrophic events. A major part of the course introduces students to the sociological aspects of disasters: Are disasters socially constructed or are they natural? How do disasters impact the social fabric of communities? How does the society respond to the disaster? Students are introduced to key concepts in disaster studies such as risk, vulnerability and resiliency and they are challenged to think about why some communities cope and recover better than others during and after disasters. Disaster models, theories and philosophical approaches, along with myths and fallacies regarding disasters are also studied. In the context of understanding disasters, political and developmental perspectives are also introduced. The final section of the course explores the current strategies for disaster management in Pakistan.
