265.Title: Introduction to Gender and Sexuality Studies
265.Description: This course will be an in-depth examination of selected topics related to sexuality, the gendered body, and cultural representations and constructions of gender. Building on knowledge and experiences provided by the quoted material, we will focus on various ways to answer the following key questions: How do we understand the sexed and gendered body in contemporary society? In what ways do heteronormative ideologies, the imposition of the gender binary, and institutionalized sexism and its intersection with other marginalized identity signifiers affect our understanding of what it means to be a woman? To be a man? To be gender fluid? To be “masculine” or “feminine?” To be gay, straight, bisexual, asexual, queer? What are possible strategies and sites of resistance to these discourses?

310.Description: This course provides an introduction to Sociological theory by focusing on the classical works of Emile Durkheim, Karl Marx, and Max Weber. We read primary texts and discuss the key theoretical and methodological themes introduced by each author. The aims are to become familiar with important perspectives on social structures and social change, and the enduring influence of each author on subsequent developments in the Social Sciences. Students are expected to acquire a solid grounding in the core concepts and foundational theoretical perspectives of Sociology by the end of the course.

346.Title: The Politics of Resources
346.Description: The Politics of ResourcesFrom Gulf oil to Indonesian timber, African blood diamonds to Sui gas, natural resources and the conflict that surrounds their control and commodification have been major sources of contention in the modern world. This course explores the historical causes and consequences of this strife, spanning all continents and employing the methods of diverse disciplines in the social sciences. The empirical scope of the course is broad, with primary data and textual materials as well as secondary readings related to case studies ranging from colonial India and the Americas to contemporary Africa and East Asia. The course begins with three weeks of introductory work to familiarise students with the conceptual frameworks and methodologies employed, and to engage them in thinking about nature and the environment as a political and sociological issue. The remainder of the course is thematically focused and structured around the distinct histories of resources themselves – land, water, oil, gas, timber, rubber, uranium, precious metals and stones. In comparing global histories of resource-commodification and conflict across time and space, we relate the physical properties of resources and technological processes involved in extraction, transport, marketization and usage to political, cultural, economic and environmental problems. These include transitions to capitalism and colonial resource regimes as well as more recent neoliberal drives to comodify ever more of the world’s natural resources. Wherever possible, case studies from Pakistan will be used to illuminate concepts and concerns. Drawing upon classical and more recent writings from across the social sciences and environmental humanities, we question the wisdom of interpretations that explain all conflict as flowing from scarcity. We also interrogate technocratic discourses about the global South’s ‘resource-curse’. Refusing simple answers to age-old questions (e.g. why does the abundance of resources rarely benefit the local communities in which they are ‘discovered’?), this course invites participants to consider the profound implications of resource-politics for regions, nations and communities in the modern period.

364.Description: This course provides students with an introduction to the field of masculinity studies—an area that has, until recently, received little attention in gender studies as a whole and in the Global South in particular. Hence, this course will provide an overview of theories related to the social construction of masculinities historically and in diverse contexts. This is an interdisciplinary course, but emphasis is placed on sociological and anthropological approaches to the study of masculinities (as opposed to biological or psychological approaches).

373.Title: "Indigenous" Knowledge(s) Through a Sociological Lens
373.Description: Knowledge as a conscious activity is an attempt to make sense of Being as a lived experience. If we look around, we find life becoming more burdensome and problematic, and part of the reason could be that the frame of reference we use to make sense of this alienating experience is flawed. It may be because, more often than note, knowledge we produce and consume across social sciences originates from the specific experiences of a white, privileged European man, which is assumed to be objective, neutral, and rational. Although the post structuralist, postmodern and constructivist turns within sociology and anthropology exposed the apparent fault lines in the objectivist, positivist, and modernist discourse of knowledge production, it nevertheless shared the underlying assumption, i.e., the universalist claims to generate knowledge that stems out of a Cartesian duality of the knower and the known. This leads to the generation of a knowledge that is devoid of any experiential reference. Therefore, such knowledge lacks any transformative capacity because it does not resonate with the experiences that people go through in their daily lives.This course is an attempt to look at various repertoires that may not share such a split between the knower and the known, between ontology and epistemology, and between the microcosm and the macrocosm. Scholars from across the world are looking for ways to engage with more localised, more embodied forms of knowledges that are embedded in other non-white, non-Eurocentric epistemological traditions. This is a survey course in which the rich strands of postcolonial, decolonial, and indigenous knowledges are visited, without assuming a break from the colonial apparatus either. The alternates need not look entirely alien to the existing or the preceding, therefore, this course starts with a clear objective to piece together an alternate lens that is neither colonial, nor post/decolonial, nor indigenous. Readings from Ramayana, Gautama Buddha, Baghat Kabir and Bulleh Shah, therefore, will be a vital component of the reimagining exercise, to shed old/new light on the worn-out conceptions of identity, subjectivity, social justice, and epistemic violence.

412.Title: Political Sociology
412.Description: Political Sociology investigates the social bases of politics and the impact of politics on society. Since World War II, and the 1960s in particular, the steady growth of interest, literature, and debate on state-society relations has translated into the constitution of Political Sociology as a subfield of Sociology and/or Political Science (the classification varies according to countries). In France, Political Sociology is considered an integral part of Political Science (along with Political Theory, Public Policy, Comparative Politics and International Relations). In UK, the London School of Economics (LSE) offers an MSc in Political Sociology, based in the department of Sociology, leading to an ample range of professions (teaching, research, public administration, social services, journalism, publishing, think tanks, NGOs, among others).After a brief introduction to Political Sociology and a discussion of its core issue, i.e. the social foundations of power, the course explores the work of Marx and Weber and how it has informed subsequent debate within political sociology. The course then analyses a variety of different political phenomena and processes, including the state and its manifestations, social cleavages and the interests and identities they generate, the roots and forms of political action, and transnational phenomena.

462.Title: Sociology of Emotions
462.Description: Understanding social existence is incomplete without studying emotions of social beings and social interactions across different contexts. “Emotions” as a subject of study moves beyond the cognitive or psychological for sociologists who examine the social nature of emotions and social reality. This course explores the place of emotions in society, providing in-depth theoretical and empirical engagement withclassical and contemporary theories on Sociology of Emotions. The course begins by tracing the theoretical tensions within classical Sociology between normative and affective understandings of social behavior, and contemporary theories that are foundational to Sociology of Emotions. The course then moves towards an exploration of core themes in this sub-discipline at the micro and macro levels of social existence and social change.

100.Title: Writing and Communication
100.Description: SS 100 is a four-credit undergraduate course designed for first year BA/BSc students at Lahore University of Management Sciences. It also accommodates students who may not have taken the course during their first year. Writing at the university level can seem like a daunting experience, so this introductory course is designed to develop students’ composition writing skills as well as their oral communication abilities – both essential to successful future university coursework. To address the first aim, we will spend the bulk of course time honing writing skills to create clear forceful prose, to formulate and support a compelling thesis, to employ rhetorical strategies effectively, and when appropriate, to observe the conventions of academic writing. To address the second aim, the course concurrently aims at developing a constructive and practical approach to effective oral communication in academic settings. Specific goals for this course include: gaining a clear sense of audience and purpose in persuasive writing and oral presentation; understanding and employing techniques of argument analysis; being awareness of style and voice; developing fluency in various aspects of the writing process, such as pre-writing, thesis development, evidence construction, critical analysis, revision techniques, and also working cooperatively with others on the final presentation project. Assignments are designed to support both course aims. Throughout the quarter students will have daily reading assignments that are meant to accompany the lecture material and they will be responsible for this material. They will write four essays, in addition to smaller written assignments and quizzes during the quarter. Finally, there will be two speaking opportunities: the first is a short, 4-5 minute presentation while the second is an extensive final presentation in groups. Also, an essential component of this class is class participation and attendance

101.Title: Islamic Studies
101.Description: This short survey course has clearly defined aims. Conversely, this means that it has its limitations too. Its overriding aim is to introduce the student to the academic study of Islam—Islam here denoting both a religious system, grounded upon certain normative revealed sources, as well as a civilization unfolding over time as a complex network of cultures shaped by historical contingencies.  In other words, it may be called as the study of the Islamic Religious Tradition. The course remains indifferent to the personal beliefs of the students, to any sectarian identity they espouse, and any doctrinal point of view they hold. The course also does not take any sides. It aims to report, as much as possible, what has been discussed within the Islamic religious tradition. We shall begin by contextualizing this course by looking at the traditions of learning and transmission of knowledge in Muslims societies, enabling students to understand the rationale and function of this course at LUMS in a better way. From there we move to the fundamental methodological question: How does one study a given religious system? What are the scholarly tools and conceptual frameworks for exploring a civilization radiating from a religious core? What are the limitations of an academic study of Islam? In what way is it different from the account and conception of the believer or, in the case of cultures, of the actor?In short, how do we approach the study of Islamic religious tradition in the modern World in a university ?From here we move on to an historical overview of the tradition. We look at the ‘doctrinal aspects including the Qur’an, Hadith, and the life of the Prophet (PBUH). We move to the ‘intellectual’ aspects exploring the legal/jurisprudential, theological and philosophical developments and discussions in the Muslim experience. Next, we delve into the spiritual realm looking at the mystical tradition of Sufism

102.Title: Pakistan Studies: Culture and Heritage
102.Description: What does it mean to think about Pakistan beyond official textbooks, narratives and nationalist timelines? This introductory course on ‘Pakistan Studies’ challenges conventional historiography by exploring Pakistan’s history through thematic questions rather than linear chronology and by engaging with narratives that probe alternative perspectives. From the ideological dreams—and critiques—surrounding its creation on the eve of independence to the everyday lived experiences and crisis shaping its postcolonial decades, the course seeks to move beyond a one-dimensional view of nationalism and a static way of thinking about the Partition and the creation of a homeland as an event frozen in time. We then move on to evaluate how the negotiation of questions of belonging and citizenship, the construction of a past and historical memory, the entrenchment of religion, the articulation of gender, the imagination of a national culture, the curation of a national literature and the rise of militarism were never fixed discourses, but contested processes embedded in the ever-evolving relationship between state and non-state actors in post-independence Pakistan. Drawing on new scholarship, students will thus reimagine how Pakistani identity has evolved by uncovering the stories that lie beneath—and stretch beyond—the surface of official history. Our focus throughout the course will be on the content of the readings with some engagement with primary sources, either introduced in the lecture or through student presentations and connected in one or more ways to a guiding question or prompt to anchor discussion and reflection.

1312.Title: Fundamentals of Raag and Taal [Vocal and Flute]
1312.Description: South Asian classical music, often referred to as Hindustani classical music, stands apart from its Western counterpart with its unique focus on ras—the emotional essence of a performance. Unlike the symphony-driven tradition of Western classical music, Hindustani music emphasizes the deep connection between sur (pitch) and laey (rhythm or tempo) to evoke profound emotions such as joy, sorrow, devotion, or exuberance. At the heart of this tradition lies the raga system, a sophisticated framework for melody, and taals, intricate rhythmic cycles that serve as the foundation for musical expression in this tradition.This course exploresthe immensely rich heritage of South Asian classical music through both vocal techniques and the unique adaptation of the bansuri (flute) into classical performance—a phenomenon that emerged less than a century ago. Flute pioneers such as Pannalal Ghosh and Hariprasad Chaurasia have revolutionized its role, transforming the bansuri into a powerful medium for classical interpretation. With a focus on the interplay of raga and taal, this course offers an immersive journey into the soundscapes of South Asian classical music.

187.Title: Applied Statistics for Humanities
187.Description: Data is often regarded as the modern world’s most precious resource. As data becomes more important, so does the need to properly analyze and interpret it. This is an introductory statistics course designed to familiarize humanities students with the basics of understanding and analyzing data. It aims to equip students with statistical and data analysis tools used in academic research or professional settings. The course will focus on practical examples from social sciences, while keeping mathematical derivations to a minimum. The course starts with an introduction to typical datasets, central tendency measures and graphing. The course will then progress to cover the basics of hypothesis testing, regression analysis and causal inference. The final part of the course will look at published material that review the concepts learned throughout the course.HSS majors will benefit by being able to understand statistics at a level that enables them to meaningfully engage with reports or papers that have made use of statistical techniques to present information.

2203.Title: Digital Approaches to the Humanities
2203.Description: Digital Approaches to the HumanitiesDigital humanities meld computational methods with hermeneutics. It is a growing field of study within the humanities that brings together computers, statistics and literary and cultural studies. As Alan Liu puts it, “the digital humanities community—which specializes in making creative use of digital technology to advance humanities research and teaching as well as to think about the basic nature of the new media and technologies—woke up to its special potential and responsibility to assist humanities advocacy”. Today, digital humanists have the potential to use new technologies to help advance humanities research and bring its scholarship to a wider audience. In this 200-level course we will focus on how computational and statistical methods are used to analyze small and large corpora of literary and cultural texts. Students will read critical texts and practical studies of applied digital humanities research to reflect on the limits and affordances of computational criticism. They will also learn to do basic programming in Python—a common programming language—to better understand the technical side of digital humanities and understand for themselves the potential of this field.
